title: What is an LLM? Tokens, Training & Temperature
description: Language models are pattern-matching machines trained on text. Here's the non-hype version of how they work.
learningObjectives: I can explain what a token is and why it matters for AI costs
I can describe how LLMs learn from training data
I can explain what temperature controls and when to change it

contentSections.title: What's actually happening when you type to Claude

contentSections.body: Alex uses Claude every day to draft emails, analyze data, and write code. But when asked 'how does it actually work?', most people shrug. Understanding the mechanism makes you a dramatically better user. You'll know when to trust it, when to push back, and why certain prompts fail.

**An LLM (Large Language Model)** is a neural network trained to predict what text comes next.

That's it. At the core, Claude is an extraordinarily sophisticated autocomplete system — trained on hundreds of billions of words — that got so good at predicting the next word that it learned to reason, code, and explain.

**Tokens** are how LLMs process text. Not characters, not words — tokens:
- `Hello` = 1 token
- `Hello, world!` = 4 tokens
- `tokenization` = 3 tokens (token / ization... roughly)
- 1000 words ≈ 750 tokens

Tokens matter because they determine:
- **Cost** — APIs charge per token
- **Context limits** — Claude can process up to ~200,000 tokens at once
- **Speed** — more tokens = slower response

contentSections.question: Why would an LLM trained on 'predicting the next word' be able to write code?
contentSections.answer: Code is text. The training data included billions of lines of code, documentation, and programming discussions. By learning to predict what comes next in code, the model learned the patterns, syntax, and logic of programming — the same way it learned the patterns of English.
contentSections.hint: Think about what the training data included beyond just regular text

contentSections.body: LLMs are next-token prediction machines. They got so good at it that reasoning emerged as a side effect. Tokens are the unit of text they process.

contentSections.scenario: You're generating code and want correct, deterministic output, not creative variation.
contentSections.question: Which temperature setting fits?

feedback.low: Right — code generation wants correct, not creative: temperature 0–0.3.
feedback.high: 0.7–1.5 is for creative writing and brainstorming — the opposite of what code generation needs.

contentSections.concept: Temperature 0 — always picks the most likely next token, deterministic. Temperature 1 — balanced. Temperature 2 — very random. Code generation: 0–0.3. Creative writing: 0.7–1.5.

contentSections.body:
**Training** is how an LLM learns. It's done once (by Anthropic), not every time you talk to Claude.

Simplified training process:
1. Take an enormous text corpus (web, books, code, papers)
2. Remove the last word from a sentence
3. Have the model guess the next word
4. Compare to the actual word — calculate error
5. Adjust billions of parameters to reduce the error
6. Repeat trillions of times

After training, the model's parameters *are* its 'memory'. It has no database to look up — everything it knows is encoded in 70+ billion numbers.

**Fine-tuning** (RLHF) shapes behavior: human raters evaluate responses, and the model learns which responses humans prefer. That's why Claude is helpful and honest, not just statistically likely.

**Why Claude doesn't 'learn' from your conversations:** Each conversation starts fresh. Claude's parameters don't change from your input. What you put in the context window is temporary — it disappears when the conversation ends.

contentSections.question: Why does Claude sometimes state false information confidently?
contentSections.answer: Claude predicts what *sounds* correct, not what *is* correct. It has no way to verify claims against reality — it only knows what was in training data. If the training data was wrong, or if a topic is outside the distribution, it predicts plausible-sounding text that may be false.
contentSections.hint: Remember: Claude is predicting the next token, not looking things up in a database

contentSections.body: Training encodes knowledge into parameters. Claude doesn't learn from your conversations. Hallucinations happen because it predicts plausible text, not verified facts.

**Temperature** controls how much randomness is in Claude's outputs.

- **Temperature 0** — always picks the most likely next token. Deterministic, predictable, sometimes repetitive.
- **Temperature 1** — balanced. Good for most tasks.
- **Temperature 2** — very random. Creative but potentially incoherent.

**When to use what:**

| Task | Temperature |
|------|-------------|
| Code generation | 0 – 0.3 (you want correct, not creative) |
| Analysis/summarization | 0.3 – 0.7 |
| Creative writing | 0.7 – 1.5 |
| Brainstorming | 1.0 – 1.5 |

In the API: `temperature: 0.7` in your request body.

*For most everyday use, you don't need to change temperature. The default (1.0) works for 90% of tasks.*

title: Attention & Context — How Claude 'Reads'
description: The transformer architecture explained for humans. How Claude weighs what matters in your message.
learningObjectives: I can explain what attention means in a transformer model
I can describe what a context window is and its practical implications
I can explain why the order and position of information in a prompt matters

contentSections.body: In 2017, a team at Google published a paper titled 'Attention Is All You Need.' It introduced the transformer architecture that powers every modern AI model. Understanding attention — even intuitively — changes how you write prompts.

**Attention** lets the model weigh how much any word in the input relates to any other word.

Old models read text left-to-right, one word at a time. Transformers can consider all words simultaneously and learn relationships between words regardless of distance.

Example: In 'The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big', what does 'it' refer to?
- An old model might guess 'suitcase' (most recent noun)
- Attention allows the model to understand 'it' refers to 'trophy' by learning that 'too big to fit' points back to the thing that didn't fit

**In practice:** Claude doesn't just read your prompt — it builds a rich map of how every word relates to every other word. That's why context in your prompt matters so much.

contentSections.question: Why does adding more relevant context to your prompt generally produce better Claude responses?
contentSections.answer: Attention lets Claude weight relevant context heavily when generating each token. More relevant information in the prompt = more signal for attention to find and leverage. Vague prompts give Claude little to attend to, so it fills gaps with defaults.
contentSections.hint: If attention weighs relationships between words, what happens when you give more relevant words?

contentSections.body: Attention is how transformers understand relationships in text. More relevant context in your prompt gives Claude more to attend to.

contentSections.scenario: "The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big."
contentSections.question: What does 'it' refer to?

options.label: The suitcase
The trophy

feedback.trophy: Right — attention lets the model learn that 'too big to fit' points back to the trophy, not just the most recent noun.
feedback.suitcase: That's what an old left-to-right model without real attention might guess — just picking the most recent noun. Attention does better.

contentSections.concept: Attention lets the model weigh how much any word in the input relates to any other word. An old model might guess 'suitcase' (most recent noun); attention allows understanding that 'it' refers to 'trophy' by learning that 'too big to fit' points back to the thing that didn't fit.

contentSections.body:
The **context window** is everything Claude can 'see' at once: your entire conversation history, the system prompt, and everything you've sent in the current session.

**Claude's context window: ~200,000 tokens (~150,000 words)**

That's roughly the length of a 500-page novel — enough for most tasks.

**Practical implications:**

1. **Recency bias** — information at the end of a long context gets more attention than information in the middle. Put important instructions at the start *and* the end.

2. **Context doesn't persist** — when the conversation ends, the context is gone. Claude has no memory between sessions unless you implement it.

3. **Fill it thoughtfully** — sending a 100-page document with one relevant paragraph wastes context and dilutes attention. Send only what's relevant.

4. **Cost scales with tokens** — long contexts cost more and take longer.

**Lost in the middle problem:** Research shows LLMs tend to lose track of information in the very middle of a long context. If you have a critical instruction, put it at the start AND remind it at the end. 'As mentioned at the start, only respond in French.'

contentSections.question: You're debugging a bug with Claude and the conversation is 50+ messages long. Claude starts giving inconsistent advice. Why?
contentSections.answer: The early context (where you described the problem) may be getting less attention as the conversation grows. Claude's recent responses dominate the context. Solution: start a fresh conversation and re-paste only the relevant context.
contentSections.hint: Think about what's happening to the context window as the conversation grows

contentSections.body: Context window = Claude's working memory. It doesn't persist between sessions. Critical info should appear at start and end of long contexts.

Position in a prompt affects how strongly Claude attends to information:

**System prompt** (if using API) — highest weight. Sets persistent context, tone, restrictions.

**Beginning of conversation** — strong signal. Claude reads the full setup before generating.

**Most recent message** — also strong signal. The immediate task.

**Middle of a long conversation** — weaker. Information can get 'lost'.

**Practical prompt structure for complex tasks:**
```
1. Role/context (start): 'You are a senior software engineer reviewing code...'
2. Task: 'Review this function for security vulnerabilities'
3. Constraints: 'Focus on: SQL injection, auth bypasses, input validation'
4. Material: [paste the code]
5. Output format (end): 'List each vulnerability with: severity, location, fix'
```

Putting the output format at the end acts as a final 'nudge' — Claude reads it right before generating, maximizing its influence.

title: Hallucinations — When Claude Makes Things Up
description: Why LLMs confidently state false things. How to spot hallucinations and build workflows that catch them.
learningObjectives: I can explain the mechanism behind AI hallucinations
I can identify common hallucination patterns in Claude outputs
I can design prompts that reduce hallucination risk

contentSections.body: Alex asked Claude to cite three research papers on transformer attention. Claude produced three citations — author names, journal names, publication years, DOIs. All three papers didn't exist. The citations were structurally perfect. Completely fabricated. This is an AI hallucination.

**Hallucination** happens when an LLM generates plausible-sounding but false information.

**Why it happens:**
Remember — Claude predicts the next most likely token. When asked for a research paper citation, the model predicts: what does a correct citation *look like*? It generates the *form* of a citation without verifying the *content* actually exists.

**Hallucination types:**

1. **Factual hallucination** — 'Claude Shannon invented the internet' (he didn't)
2. **Citation hallucination** — made-up paper titles, authors, DOIs
3. **Code hallucination** — functions or libraries that don't exist
4. **Numeric hallucination** — wrong statistics, dates, percentages
5. **Entity hallucination** — wrong details about real people or places

**Confidence doesn't correlate with accuracy.** Claude is equally confident when right and wrong. That's what makes it dangerous.

contentSections.question: Why are citation hallucinations particularly common and dangerous?
contentSections.answer: Citations have a very consistent format that Claude learned well — author (year) journal vol(issue):pages. So it generates *structurally correct* citations even when the content is invented. Dangerous because they look authoritative — readers may not check if they actually exist.
contentSections.hint: Think about the pattern of a citation vs. its content

contentSections.body: Hallucinations happen because LLMs generate plausible text, not verified facts. High confidence ≠ correct. Always verify factual claims.

contentSections.scenario: Alex asked Claude to cite three research papers on transformer attention. Claude produced three citations — author names, journal names, publication years, DOIs. All three papers didn't exist.
contentSections.question: Why did this happen?

options.label: Claude intentionally deceived Alex
Claude predicted what a citation looks like, without verifying the content exists

feedback.form-not-content: Right — Claude predicts the next most likely token. Asked for a citation, it predicts what a correct citation looks like, generating the form without verifying the content actually exists.
feedback.intentional: Not intentional — there's no deception here, just next-token prediction generating a plausible-looking form without any fact-checking step.

contentSections.mechanism: Hallucination happens when an LLM generates plausible-sounding but false information. Confidence doesn't correlate with accuracy — Claude is equally confident when right and wrong. That's what makes it dangerous.

contentSections.body:
**Red flags that suggest hallucination:**
- Specific numbers/statistics without a clear source
- Quotes attributed to real people you haven't heard before
- Library names or API methods you can't find in docs
- Dates that sound too precise ('on March 14th, 1987')
- Any claim that's easy to verify but you haven't checked

**Reducing hallucinations in your prompts:**

```
# Instead of:
'What are the latest statistics on remote work adoption?'

# Try:
'I know your training has a cutoff. What were the approximate statistics on
remote work adoption as of your knowledge cutoff? Flag any claims
you're uncertain about.'
```

```
# For code:
'Only use Node.js 18 built-in APIs. If you're using a third-party library,
explicitly say so and I'll verify it exists before implementing.'
```

**Ground Claude with context:** Paste the actual documentation, data, or source material and ask Claude to work *only* from that.
**Never trust Claude for:** medical dosages, legal citations, financial figures, academic citations, or anything where being wrong has real consequences. Always verify against primary sources.

contentSections.question: How does providing source material (like pasting documentation) reduce hallucinations?
contentSections.answer: When you paste the actual source, Claude can attend to real text when generating its response, rather than reconstructing from memory. It's the difference between open-book and closed-book — the real text in context reduces reliance on pattern-matching from training.
contentSections.hint: Think about how attention works — what happens when the right content is in the context window?

contentSections.body: Reduce hallucinations by: asking Claude to flag uncertainty, grounding with source material, using temperature 0 for factual tasks.

Build hallucination checks into your workflows:

**For code:**
1. Claude writes code → run it, don't just review it
2. Test edge cases, not just the happy path
3. Any library you've never heard of → check it on npm/PyPI before using

**For factual content:**
1. Ask Claude to add `[VERIFY]` tags to claims it's uncertain about
2. Spot-check 3-5 specific facts per response
3. For important documents, cross-reference with a second source

**For citations:**
1. Always verify paper existence via Google Scholar or DOI lookup
2. Better: paste the abstract and ask Claude to work from *that*
3. Never cite a Claude-generated citation without verifying

**Ask Claude to reason about its confidence:**
*'On a scale of 1-10, how confident are you in each of these claims? Flag the ones under 7 for me to verify.'*

title: Claude's Limits — What It Doesn't Know
description: Knowledge cutoffs, context degradation, training biases. Be a sophisticated user, not a naive one.
learningObjectives: I can identify what types of knowledge Claude reliably doesn't have
I can explain how training data biases affect Claude's outputs
I can design prompts that work within Claude's limitations

contentSections.body: Marcus asked Claude about the latest React release. Claude gave a confident, detailed answer — about a version that was already 18 months old. Knowledge cutoffs are invisible unless you know to look for them.

**Knowledge cutoff**: Claude's training data has an end date. Events, releases, research, and changes after that date are unknown to Claude.

This affects:
- **Tech**: Library versions, new APIs, framework features, security vulnerabilities
- **News**: Events, company changes, political outcomes
- **Research**: Papers published after cutoff, updated guidelines
- **Prices**: Costs, salary data, market figures

**How to work with it:**

```
# Always clarify when the topic is time-sensitive:
'I know your training has a cutoff. Give me your best knowledge
as of when you were trained. I'll check for recent updates separately.'

# For tech stacks:
'I'm using [library name] version [X.X]. Work within
this version's API — don't suggest features from newer versions.'

# Ground with current info:
[Paste the current docs/changelog]
'Based on the above documentation, help me...'
```

contentSections.question: You ask Claude to help you write a cover letter for a job at a company. What should you verify about Claude's knowledge?
contentSections.answer: Recent news: company might have had layoffs, changed direction, or been acquired. Leadership: CEO or team may have changed. Products: new or discontinued offerings. Culture: recent employee reviews or glassdoor ratings. Claude's knowledge might be months or years out of date on all of these.
contentSections.hint: What changes about companies over time that Claude might not know?

contentSections.body: Claude's knowledge has an expiry date. Always ask yourself: 'Could this have changed since training?' If yes, verify.

contentSections.title: Training biases — what's over- and under-represented

contentSections.body:
Claude's training data wasn't a perfect sample of human knowledge. Some things are overrepresented, some underrepresented.

**Overrepresented:**
- English (vs. other languages)
- Western perspectives (US/Europe-centric defaults)
- Tech culture (developer, startup, Silicon Valley norms)
- Certain time periods (very recent years before cutoff)
- Formal/academic writing styles

**Underrepresented:**
- Non-English cultures and perspectives
- Oral traditions and indigenous knowledge
- Lived experience of disability, poverty, marginalization
- Regional or domain-specific knowledge
- Specialized expert knowledge in narrow fields

**Practical effect:** Claude gives better answers about JavaScript than Lua, about San Francisco startups than about small businesses in rural India, about academic psychology than about traditional healing practices.

**Mitigation:** Provide explicit context about your situation. Claude adapts — it just doesn't assume non-default contexts.

**For Bedcoders specifically:** Claude may have less knowledge about accessibility needs, chronic illness constraints, and disability-friendly design patterns than it does about mainstream tech culture. Always review Claude's output through your own lens.

contentSections.question: Sarah asks Claude to suggest 'good productivity tools for a freelancer.' The response focuses on standing desks and commute time. What might explain this?
contentSections.answer: Claude's default assumption of 'freelancer' is likely someone without accessibility constraints, working standard hours at a desk. It didn't account for working from bed, chronic fatigue, or variable energy. Mitigation: add explicit context — 'I work from bed due to chronic illness, need tools for variable energy levels.'
contentSections.hint: What's the default assumption baked into the training data about freelancers?

contentSections.body: Training biases create default assumptions. Override them with explicit context. Claude adapts when you tell it to.

contentSections.title: What Claude is genuinely good and bad at

contentSections.scenario: Claude's training data wasn't a perfect sample of human knowledge — some things are overrepresented, some underrepresented.
contentSections.question: Which of these areas does Claude have a real training-data advantage in?

items.label: English-language content
Western (US/Europe-centric) perspectives
Tech, startup, and developer culture
Oral traditions and indigenous knowledge
Lived experience of disability, poverty, or marginalization
Small businesses in rural India

explanation.english: Overrepresented — English dominates the training data relative to other languages.
explanation.western: Overrepresented — US/Europe-centric defaults show up unless you specify otherwise.
explanation.tech-culture: Overrepresented — developer, startup, Silicon Valley norms are heavily represented.
explanation.oral-traditions: Underrepresented — oral traditions and indigenous knowledge are among the least-represented areas.
explanation.disability-experience: Underrepresented — lived experience of disability, poverty, and marginalization is underrepresented.
explanation.rural-india: Underrepresented — regional, non-Western small-business context isn't well covered.

contentSections.synthesis: Claude gives better answers about JavaScript than Lua, about San Francisco startups than about small businesses in rural India, about academic psychology than about traditional healing practices. The mitigation: provide explicit context about your situation — Claude adapts, it just doesn't assume non-default contexts.

contentSections.body:
**Very strong:**
- Common programming patterns and popular languages
- Explanation, summarization, paraphrasing
- Writing (emails, docs, copy) with style guidance
- Brainstorming and ideation
- Reasoning through a problem step by step
- Debugging with error messages and code context

**Moderate (verify carefully):**
- Specific framework versions and features
- Numerical reasoning and math
- Medical/legal/financial information
- Country-specific regulations and practices

**Weak (always verify):**
- Real-time information
- Highly specialized domain knowledge
- Novel research not in training data
- Anything that requires looking something up
- Exact numbers, statistics, citations

title: The whole mechanism in one sentence, then unpacked
description: The entire generative mechanism, stated once and then taken apart: predict the next token given everything before it, append it, repeat.

learningObjectives.text: State the complete next-token-prediction mechanism in one sentence
Explain what autoregressive generation does and does not imply about planning
Predict which of two candidate continuations a model is more likely to produce

contentSections.body:
You type "Roses are red, violets are" into a chat window. Before you finish reading this sentence, it has already answered "blue."

It didn't recall a poem. It doesn't have a memory of nursery rhymes it "knows." It did one specific, mechanical thing, and it is the only thing it ever does — the rest of this lesson is taking that one thing apart.

contentSections.question: In one sentence: what is a language model doing, mechanically, every single time it produces a word?
contentSections.answer: Computing a probability distribution over every possible next token, given all the tokens so far, then picking one — and repeating that, one token at a time, until it stops.
contentSections.hint: Think about what has to happen between you hitting enter and the first word of the reply appearing — not what the reply eventually says.

contentSections.body:
That's the whole mechanism: **given everything so far, predict what token comes next; append it; repeat.** Everything else — the fact that replies read as fluent paragraphs, that they seem to stay on topic, that they can hold a conversation across many turns — is that one operation, run thousands of times in a row, each prediction conditioned on its own previous output as well as your prompt. This is what "autoregressive" means: the model's own past predictions become part of the input to its next prediction. It is writing one token, reading its own sentence back including the word it just wrote, and asking again "what's most likely to come after *this*."

There is no separate planning stage that runs first and decides where the sentence is going to end up. The token that arrives fifth is chosen without any commitment to what the fifteenth token will be — it only looks like there was a plan because, for most ordinary text, predicting well token-by-token *produces* coherent-looking output, the same way a person humming a familiar tune note-by-note produces a recognizable song without consciously rehearsing the ending in advance.

contentSections.question: Put the actual generation loop in the order it really runs, for producing one single token of a reply:
steps: Take the sequence of tokens so far (your prompt plus anything generated already)
Compute a probability score for every token in the vocabulary being the next one
Select one token, weighted by those probabilities
Append the selected token to the sequence
Repeat the whole loop for the next token, now including the one just added
contentSections.explanation: Notice step 4 feeds directly back into step 1 — the token the model just wrote becomes part of "the sequence so far" for the very next prediction. That feedback loop is the entire mechanism of autoregressive generation. There's no step anywhere in this loop labelled "decide what the response is really about" — if that quality shows up, it's an emergent effect of doing this loop well, not a separate stage that ran first.

contentSections.body: Every token a model produces, including the ones that sound most like reasoning, is a sample from a probability distribution computed one step at a time — nothing more privileged is running underneath.

contentSections.title: What that one sentence rules in and out

contentSections.body: Ask a model "what's 47 times 89?" and a lot of the time it gets it right. Ask it "what's 8,472,013 times 5,991,204?" and it usually doesn't, even though both are the same operation. If it's just predicting the next likely token, how does it get *either* one right?

contentSections.scenario: A model answers small multiplication problems correctly most of the time, and gets noticeably worse as the numbers get larger — not randomly wrong, but wrong in a way that looks like a rough estimate rather than a random guess.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely explanation, given that the model has no calculator built in and is fundamentally predicting tokens?

options.label: It secretly runs real arithmetic in the background for small numbers only
It learned patterns from huge amounts of arithmetic-shaped text, which generalize well for short problems and break down as the pattern gets less like anything it saw enough of
It's guessing randomly every time, and short numbers happen to be right more often by chance

feedback.secret-calc: There's no hidden calculator in a plain language model — every digit it outputs is still a predicted token. (Some products *do* wire a real calculator or code interpreter in behind the scenes as a separate tool; that's a deliberate add-on covered later, not something the base mechanism does on its own.)
feedback.pattern-generalize: Right. Training data is full of worked arithmetic — times tables, textbook examples, code, homework answers — so the model has learned strong token-level patterns for short, common problems. Those patterns generalize reasonably well to nearby unseen problems. But an eight-digit multiplication doesn't resemble anything memorable in the training data closely enough for those patterns to carry it reliably, so the answer degrades toward something that merely *looks like* a plausible-magnitude number.
feedback.random: It's not random — you can watch the errors: they're usually close in magnitude to the right answer, not wildly off. A model firing random tokens for digits would look nothing like that. The near-misses are the signature of pattern completion, not noise.

contentSections.mechanism: **Prediction from learned patterns is not the same operation as calculation, and it degrades differently.** A calculator is either exactly right or catastrophically wrong (overflow, wrong button). A predictor is right where it's seen enough similar shapes, and gracefully worse the further a problem sits from anything it learned patterns for. That graceful-worse curve, not a hard cliff, is itself evidence that arithmetic is being predicted, not computed.

contentSections.body:
This is what the one-sentence mechanism does and doesn't rule out. It doesn't mean the model has *memorized* every sentence it can produce — that's obviously impossible; there are more possible eight-word sentences than there are training documents. What it learned instead is something more general: statistical regularities about which tokens tend to follow which other tokens, abstracted enough that it produces sensible output for inputs it has never seen verbatim. That generalization is genuinely powerful — powerful enough to look, most of the time, indistinguishable from understanding.

What the mechanism *does* rule out is any separate step that checks the output against reality before it's produced. Nothing in "predict the next token" includes "and verify this is true first." Fluency and correctness are computed by the same process and are not coupled to each other — which is the reason a model can say something false in exactly the same confident, well-formed sentence structure it uses to say something true. That isn't a glitch layered on top of the mechanism. It's what the mechanism, honestly described, predicts about itself.

contentSections.scenario: Someone claims all of the following follow from "a language model is just predicting the next token."
contentSections.question: Which of these are genuine consequences of pure next-token prediction, with no separate fact-checking step?

items.label: It can state something false in exactly the same confident tone it uses for something true
It has no built-in way to flag its own uncertainty, unless it was specifically trained to produce hedging language in situations like this one
It can only ever reproduce sentences that already existed somewhere in its training data
A longer, more detailed-sounding answer is not automatically a more accurate one

explanation.confident-wrong: Correct — nothing in the mechanism attaches a truth-check to token selection, so tone and confidence are generated by the same process regardless of whether the content is accurate.
explanation.no-self-uncertainty: Correct — any hedging ("I'm not certain, but...") is itself just more predicted text, produced because similar situations in training data were often followed by hedging language, not because the model consulted an internal confidence meter.
explanation.cant-be-novel: This is the one that doesn't follow, and it's tempting because "it learned from existing text" sounds like "it can only repeat existing text." It's false: the model generalizes patterns and routinely produces token sequences that never appeared anywhere in training, including this exact sentence.
explanation.length-not-accuracy: Correct — length and detail are style properties the model can produce fluently regardless of whether the underlying content is right, precisely because style and truth are not coupled in the mechanism.

contentSections.synthesis: The through-line: everything that's a genuine consequence traces back to one fact — nothing checks the output against the world before it's produced. The one false claim ("can only reproduce existing text") confuses *learning from* examples with *copying* them, which is a different thing generalization specifically avoids.

contentSections.body: The mechanism explains the fluency and the failure mode with the same sentence: it is optimizing for what comes next, not for what's true.

title: Tokens: how text gets chopped up
description: The model's actual unit of reading and writing is the token, not the letter or the word — and that single fact explains a whole category of otherwise-baffling failures.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what a token is and how subword tokenization splits text
Predict roughly how a given string will be tokenized

contentSections.body: Ask a model how many letter r's are in "strawberry" and, for a long stretch of models, the answer was wrong — confidently. Not a rare glitch; a famous, reproducible one. The mechanism from lesson one explains it completely, once you know what the model is actually reading.

contentSections.scenario: Most tokenizers used by current language models split common English words into surprisingly few pieces.
contentSections.question: Roughly how many tokens does a typical BPE-style tokenizer split the single word "strawberry" into?
contentSections.explanation: Around 2 — commonly something like "straw" and "berry," though the exact split depends on the specific tokenizer. The model never sees "s," "t," "r," "a"... as separate units here; it sees two chunks. Counting the letter "r" inside "strawberry" means correctly reconstructing letter-level information that got compressed away at the tokenization step — something the model has to infer indirectly rather than read off directly, which is precisely why it's unreliable.

contentSections.body:
Language models don't read text one character at a time, and they don't read it one whole word at a time either. They read **tokens** — chunks somewhere in between, produced by an algorithm (most commonly a variant of byte-pair encoding, or BPE) that was run once, in advance, over a huge amount of text to find which character sequences occur together often enough to deserve their own single unit.

The result: common short words ("the," "cat," "is") usually get one token each. Longer or rarer words get split into a small number of frequent sub-pieces — a made-up brand name, an unusual technical term, or a word in a script the tokenizer saw less of during its own training might get split into many small pieces, sometimes down to individual characters or bytes in the worst case. The model's entire notion of "what letters are inside this word" has to be reconstructed from patterns over these chunks — it isn't given to the model directly, the way it is given to you when you read the printed letters.

contentSections.code:
User: How many times does the letter 'e' appear in "bookkeeper"?
Model: The letter 'e' appears 2 times in "bookkeeper".

(The correct count is 4.)
contentSections.question: Given everything so far in this lesson, what's the single most accurate diagnosis of this specific kind of error?

options.label: The model doesn't know the alphabet
"Bookkeeper" is tokenized into a small number of subword chunks, and counting a specific letter requires inferring character-level detail the model doesn't directly have access to from those chunks
The model is deliberately being unhelpful on tedious tasks

contentSections.flawExplanation: It knows the alphabet fine in the sense that it can spell words correctly, discuss letters, and often even get *short* counting tasks right by pattern-matching on common examples seen during training. The failure is specific to tasks that require exact character-level counting inside longer or unusually-tokenized words — a repeated-letter word like "bookkeeper," split into a couple of subword chunks, requires the model to correctly reconstruct exactly which letters and how many of each live inside chunks it never sees decomposed. It's not laziness and it's not total ignorance of letters — it's a mismatch between the task (character counting) and the unit the model actually operates on (tokens).

contentSections.body: The model's unit of thought is the token, not the letter or the word — tasks that need exact letter-level attention are fighting the grain of how it reads.

Two support tickets, same length in characters, same content translated faithfully — one in English, one in Japanese. They are very unlikely to cost the same number of tokens, and token count is what both your bill and your context window are actually measured in.

contentSections.question: For most widely-used tokenizers, which typically uses more tokens to express the same amount of meaning: English text, or text in a script that was rarer in the tokenizer's own training data (many non-Latin scripts, for the tokenizers in common use)?
contentSections.answer: The rarer-script text — often by a large margin (sometimes two to three times as many tokens for equivalent meaning), because the tokenizer's vocabulary of efficient multi-character chunks was built from a corpus that skewed toward English and other well-represented languages.
contentSections.hint: A tokenizer's chunks come from whatever text it was built on — think about what happens to a script that text was scarce in.

contentSections.body: This isn't a footnote — it has real consequences. Context windows (how much a model can "see" at once, covered in depth next module) are measured in tokens, not words or characters, so the same conversation can consume noticeably different amounts of a model's available context depending on language, formatting, and vocabulary. Pricing, almost universally, is per token in and per token out. Whitespace, punctuation, capitalization and even leading spaces can each become their own token or change which token a word turns into — " hello" and "hello" and "Hello" are not guaranteed to tokenize the same way. Code and rare technical jargon frequently fragment into many small tokens, which is part of why long code files eat context faster than their character count alone would suggest.

contentSections.scenario:
Four short strings, about to be sent to a model:

1. "the quick brown fox"
2. "xk7#9zQmPv2" (a randomly generated API key)
3. "見積書を送ってください" (a Japanese sentence)
4. "def calculate_shipping_cost(weight_kg, zone):" (a line of Python)
contentSections.question: Which of these is most likely to tokenize the *least* efficiently — using the most tokens relative to its actual character count?

options.label: The plain English sentence
The random API key
The Japanese sentence
The Python code

feedback.english: Common English words are exactly what most tokenizers were built to compress efficiently — this is close to the best case, not the worst.
feedback.apikey: Right. Random alphanumeric strings have no recognizable word-pieces at all — there's no statistical regularity for the tokenizer's vocabulary to exploit, so it frequently falls back toward much shorter chunks, sometimes close to one token per character. A 12-character random key can easily cost more tokens than a 12-character common word.
feedback.japanese: This will likely tokenize less efficiently than the English example, for the reasons discussed above — but a script the tokenizer has meaningful (if smaller) training exposure to usually still gets some useful multi-character chunking, unlike a genuinely random string with zero learnable structure.
feedback.code: Code fragments often, but not always, worse than plain English due to symbols, indentation and identifiers — but common keywords (def, return) and frequent patterns still compress reasonably. Structure exists here, which is exactly what's missing from a random key.

contentSections.concept: **Tokenization efficiency tracks how much statistical regularity a string has relative to what the tokenizer was built on — not its length, its language status alone, or how meaningful it is to a human.** Structure and frequency in the training corpus is what buys compact tokens; true randomness, and to a lesser extent underrepresented scripts, buys expensive ones.

contentSections.body: Whatever you send a model — a prompt, a document, a language — costs tokens according to how well it matches the patterns its tokenizer was built on, not according to how long it looks to you.

title: Why it can write fluently about something it has wrong
description: Fluency and correctness are produced by the same process and are not coupled — this lesson works through why that produces confident, well-formed statements that happen to be false.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why fabricated content can be as fluent as accurate content
Identify the conditions (obscurity, precision, pressure to answer) most likely to produce fabrication

contentSections.title: Fluent and wrong at the same time

contentSections.body: A real incident: lawyers filed a brief full of case citations a model had invented — real-sounding case names, real-sounding courts, correctly formatted, entirely fictional. The brief read exactly like every other well-written legal brief. That's not a coincidence; it's the mechanism working as designed, aimed at the wrong target.

contentSections.scenario: A model is asked to cite supporting case law for a legal argument. It produces three citations in perfect legal format. Two are real cases that say roughly what's claimed. One is entirely fabricated — the case doesn't exist — but is formatted identically to the other two.
contentSections.question: Why would a fabricated citation be formatted just as correctly as the real ones, instead of looking obviously different?

options.label: The model has a separate "fabrication mode" it switches into for made-up content
Formatting a citation and verifying a citation exists are two unrelated capabilities — the model is fluent at the first and has no mechanism at all for the second
The model copies the format from the two real citations and applies it to the fake one deliberately

feedback.fab-mode: There's no such mode — the model runs the exact same next-token prediction process regardless of whether the content turns out to be accurate. It doesn't know, while generating, that this particular citation is fabricated.
feedback.decoupled: Right. "What does a legal citation look like" is an extremely well-supported pattern in legal training text — the model learned it thoroughly. "Does this specific case exist in reality" is not a pattern in text at all; it's a fact about the world that would require an external lookup the base mechanism doesn't perform. The two are entirely separate capabilities, and the model only has one of them.
feedback.copies: It's not applying a format from the two real citations specifically — it's generating each one independently from the same general pattern for what citations look like, learned from vast amounts of legal text, not from the two neighboring examples in this particular reply.

contentSections.mechanism: **Producing correct-looking form and producing true content are different jobs, and only one of them is what next-token prediction is built to do.** Form (grammar, formatting, structure, tone) is learned extremely well because it's consistent and repeated everywhere in training data. Truth about a specific, checkable fact requires verification against reality — a step the mechanism doesn't include unless a separate tool is deliberately wired in to do it.

contentSections.body: It helps to say this plainly: hallucination isn't a separate malfunction bolted onto an otherwise-truthful system. It's what you'd predict from the mechanism itself, once you take the one-sentence description seriously. A model trained to produce plausible continuations of text will, when asked something it lacks strong signal for, still produce a plausible continuation — because that's the only thing it knows how to do. Whether that continuation happens to be true is not a variable the mechanism tracks.

contentSections.code:
User: Can you give me the exact ISO 9001 clause number that requires a documented supplier onboarding checklist?

Model: Yes — that's specifically covered under ISO 9001:2015, Clause 8.4.3(f), which mandates a documented supplier onboarding checklist as part of the purchasing control process.
contentSections.question: This answer is fluent, specific, and confidently stated. What's the actual tell that it needs independent verification before you rely on it?

options.label: The clause number and letter sub-point are suspiciously precise for a question this specific, with no hedge or citation offered
The phrasing "Yes — that's specifically covered under" is grammatically unusual
ISO standards are never discussed by language models at all

contentSections.flawExplanation: The grammar is fine — that's exactly the point. A confident, precisely-numbered, unhedged answer to a narrow, specific standards question, delivered with no source and no uncertainty marker, is a textbook shape for a plausible-but-unverified answer: standards documents are exactly the kind of specific, checkable, low-frequency detail that training data covers unevenly, and a model under no obligation to say "I'm not sure" will still produce a specific-sounding number rather than admit the gap. (The actual clause referenced here does not correspond to that requirement — it's a fabricated but plausible-format citation, same mechanism as the legal case.) The fix isn't refusing to ask; it's treating narrow, precise, checkable claims as a category that needs the actual document open beside the answer.

contentSections.body: A fabricated answer and an accurate one are produced by the identical process — nothing about how confident or well-formed a statement sounds tells you which one you got.

contentSections.title: Where fabrication is most likely to show up

contentSections.body: Not every question is equally risky. Ask "what's the capital of France" and a model will get it right essentially every time. Ask for the exact page number of a specific claim in a specific obscure paper and the risk climbs sharply. The mechanism explains the difference.

contentSections.scenario: You're deciding which kinds of requests to independently verify before trusting a model's answer.
contentSections.question: Which of these genuinely raise the risk of a fabricated but confident answer?

items.label: The topic is obscure or minor, with little repeated coverage in typical training text
You're asking for an exact number, date, quote, or citation rather than a general description
The question is phrased in a way that implies an answer must exist ("which specific clause covers this") rather than allowing for "there may not be one"
The conversation has been going on for a long time before this question is asked

explanation.obscure-topic: Correct — low, inconsistent training coverage means weak signal for the specific fact, while the general shape of a confident answer remains just as available as ever.
explanation.exact-precision: Correct — general descriptions have lots of room to be approximately right; a specific number or quote is either exactly right or fabricated, with no safe middle ground, and precision is exactly what training data has patchiest coverage of for minor facts.
explanation.forced-answer: Correct — a question phrased to presuppose an answer exists nudges the model toward producing something answer-shaped rather than a plausible "I don't have reliable information on that." How a question is asked measurably affects this.
explanation.long-conversation: This one doesn't reliably predict fabrication risk on its own — a long conversation about consistently well-covered topics carries about the same risk as a short one. (Long conversations do have a different, real risk — covered in the context module next — but it isn't specifically about fabrication.)

contentSections.synthesis: The pattern across the three real risk factors: they all reduce the strength and consistency of the training signal, or push the model toward producing an answer regardless of whether it has one. None of them are about how the model "feels" — the model has no feeling of certainty to report.

contentSections.body: None of this means treat every answer as suspect equally — that would waste the tool. It means calibrate verification effort to these actual risk factors, the same way you'd calibrate trust in a person: you'd double-check a colleague's confident guess about an obscure statistic from memory more than their statement of something you know they check every day. The model doesn't have days it checks things on. It has training data density, and that density is exactly what these risk factors track.
Fabrication risk isn't random — it climbs with obscurity, precision, and pressure to produce an answer, because all three are exactly where training signal gets thin.

title: What "it doesn't know anything" does and doesn't mean
description: A phrase that's half right and gets repeated as though it's entirely right — this lesson separates what's genuinely true about it from what it overclaims.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish what a model's weights do and don't encode
Evaluate claims of the form "it doesn't really know X" for which part is accurate

contentSections.body: "It doesn't actually know anything, it's just predicting the next word" gets said constantly, often by people trying to sound appropriately skeptical. It's not wrong, exactly. It's also not the whole story, and treating it as the whole story leads to bad predictions about what these systems can and can't do.

contentSections.scenario:
Four statements, all using some version of "the model doesn't know X":

**A.** "It doesn't know whether what it just said is true — nothing checks."
**B.** "It doesn't know anything about chemistry, so it can't be useful for chemistry questions."
**C.** "It doesn't know where a specific fact came from — it can't cite its actual source."
**D.** "It doesn't know what happened after its training data was collected."
contentSections.question: Which of these is the one overreaching claim — the one that doesn't actually follow from the mechanism?

options.label: A — about truth-checking
B — about being useless for a whole subject
C — about not being able to cite sources
D — about the training cutoff

feedback.a: This one is accurate and important — there genuinely is no truth-checking step in the base mechanism, which is exactly what the previous lesson worked through.
feedback.b: Right — this is the overreach. "No verified fact-store" doesn't mean "no useful learned structure." A model trained on huge amounts of accurate chemistry text has learned patterns that correlate strongly with correct chemistry, and is routinely useful for chemistry questions precisely because that training signal was strong and consistent — this is covered further in the next module. "Doesn't really know" in the technical sense doesn't imply "can't be useful," and conflating the two throws away real capability.
feedback.c: Accurate — a model producing a citation is predicting citation-shaped text, not retrieving a record of where it actually learned a fact, which is why fabricated citations (previous lesson) are possible at all.
feedback.d: Accurate, and covered in depth in the training module — there's a hard boundary past which the model has no signal at all, because nothing after that point was in its training data.

contentSections.concept: **"Doesn't know" is precise about the absence of a verified, sourced, self-aware fact-checking process — and imprecise if it's stretched into a claim about how much useful, accurate structure is actually encoded.** Those are different claims, and only one of them follows from the mechanism.

contentSections.body: What's actually in the weights is compressed statistical structure over enormous amounts of text — much of which was true, well-written, and internally consistent. That structure genuinely correlates with reality across huge swaths of common knowledge, which is exactly why these systems are useful at all rather than being expensive random-text generators. Saying "it doesn't know anything" as a way of saying "none of that structure is real or useful" throws out the actual capability along with the (correct) point about the absence of verification.

"Doesn't know" is accurate about the missing verification step, and false if it's stretched into a claim that nothing accurate is encoded — the useful move is separating those two claims every time you hear the phrase.

contentSections.title: Why this distinction matters in practice

contentSections.body: Two people, same evidence, opposite conclusions: one dismisses the model entirely as "just statistics," the other trusts it uncritically because "it clearly knows so much." Both are reacting to the same half-true phrase from different directions.

contentSections.scenario: You're deciding how much to trust a model's answer on a topic you don't personally know well.
contentSections.question: Which of these are the right things to actually weigh, given everything covered so far in this module?

items.label: How consistently and widely this general topic is likely to be covered in typical training text
Whether you're asking for a general explanation or an exact, specific, checkable detail
Whether the model "sounds" confident or hesitant in this particular reply
Whether the claim is something you could independently verify cheaply if it mattered

explanation.coverage-density: Directly relevant — this is the actual driver of whether the model's learned patterns are strong for this topic, established across this whole module.
explanation.precision-asked: Directly relevant — the previous lesson's core lesson: general description versus exact precise detail is one of the strongest predictors of fabrication risk.
explanation.model-feeling: Not relevant on its own — a model's stated confidence is generated by the same fluency mechanism regardless of whether the content is accurate, so tone tells you almost nothing by itself.
explanation.verifiability: Relevant practically — even without changing what the model did, knowing you can cheaply check a claim changes how much weight you should put on trusting it unverified.

contentSections.synthesis: None of these are about the model's inner state, because it doesn't have one to report accurately. They're all about the training data and the task — which is exactly what the mechanism from this whole module says actually determines reliability.

contentSections.body: Trust the topic's coverage and the specificity of the ask, not the model's tone — tone is generated the same way whether or not the content is right.

title: The analogies that mislead, and why
description: Autocomplete, search engine, calculator, a thinking mind — every common analogy for a language model gets something right and something dangerously wrong. This lesson sorts out which is which.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate common analogies for language models against the actual mechanism
Predict specific wrong expectations each analogy would produce

contentSections.body: "It's just autocomplete." "It's basically a search engine." "It's thinking, like we do, just faster." All three get repeated constantly, often by confident people. All three are wrong in a specific, predictable way — and interestingly, all three are also *right* in a specific way.

contentSections.code: Claim: "A language model is essentially a very sophisticated search engine — you ask it a question, and it finds and returns the answer from what it learned."
contentSections.question: What's the precise flaw in this analogy, stated as specifically as possible?

options.label: Search engines are older technology, so the comparison is outdated

It implies a retrieval step against real, checkable documents — but the model generates new token sequences from learned patterns, with no retrieval and no guaranteed real source behind any given claim
Search engines are free and language models cost money

contentSections.flawExplanation: "Finds and returns" is the load-bearing phrase, and it's exactly wrong — a search engine's core operation is retrieval: locate an actual existing document and hand it to you, unchanged, traceable back to its source. A model's core operation, established across this whole module, is generation: predict a plausible next token given the current sequence, with nothing that guarantees — or even checks — a real source behind the result. Believe the search-engine analogy literally and you'll expect a model's answer to be traceable and checkable the way a search result is. It isn't, by default.

contentSections.body: Here's the general shape worth noticing: every popular analogy for a language model takes one true fact about the mechanism and generalizes it past where it holds. "It's just autocomplete" correctly identifies the core operation (predict the next unit) and incorrectly implies that scale doesn't change what that operation produces — it clearly does, which is exactly why a phone keyboard and a frontier language model, running conceptually similar operations, are not remotely similar in what they can do. "It's thinking like a person" correctly identifies that the output can be sophisticated and context-sensitive, and incorrectly implies persistent goals, beliefs, and memory that the mechanism simply doesn't have.
Every common analogy for a language model gets the surface right and the boundary wrong — the useful move is asking specifically where each one would lead you to a false expectation.

contentSections.title: What each wrong expectation actually costs you

contentSections.body: This isn't just a semantic argument. Believing the wrong analogy leads to concrete, avoidable mistakes — trusting an unsourced claim like a search result, or expecting a model to remember a correction it has no mechanism to retain.

contentSections.scenario: You're choosing which mental model to actually rely on when using an AI tool day to day.
contentSections.question: Which of these are genuine, practical costs of picking the wrong analogy — not just abstract inaccuracies?

items.label: Trusting a model's self-reported source the way you'd trust a search engine's linked result
Expecting a correction you made last week to still apply in a brand-new conversation
Assuming nothing it produces could possibly be worth taking seriously because "it's just predicting text"
Expecting the model to take noticeably longer on harder questions the way a person visibly pauses to think

explanation.trust-citation: A real cost — established directly in the previous lesson with the fabricated legal citations, which is exactly the search-engine analogy failing in practice.
explanation.expect-memory: A real cost, and it's the thinking-analogy failure — there's no persistent belief state between separate conversations, covered fully in the next module.
explanation.dismiss-capability: A real cost in the other direction — dismissing genuinely useful, well-calibrated output because the mechanism sounds unimpressive when described minimally, which throws away real capability the same way lesson four's overreach did.
explanation.expect-slow: This one doesn't actually follow, and it's worth naming why: response time is set by computation (how many tokens are generated, including any hidden reasoning steps) and system load, not by anything resembling deliberation effort scaling with difficulty the way a person's visible pause does. A trivial question and a hard one can take about the same wall-clock time.

contentSections.synthesis: The three real costs all trace back to the same root: an analogy borrowed a property (traceability, memory, or plausible-sounding-therefore-worthless) that the mechanism doesn't actually have, in either direction. The one non-cost is a surface behavior (visible pausing) that was never implied by the mechanism at all — it's just a habit of imagining the model as more human than the analogy itself even claims.

contentSections.body: No analogy is good enough to replace the actual mechanism — use one to get oriented, then check your expectations against what predicting the next token, at scale, actually implies.

title: Practice — Predict the Model's Behaviour in Eight Situations
description: Eight drills applying the module's mechanism to new situations. No new concepts — this is where the mechanism stops being something you read about and becomes something you can predict from.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the prediction mechanism to forecast model behaviour in unfamiliar situations
Rank situations by fabrication risk using training-signal strength and precision

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Eight drills across the module's ideas, ordered roughly from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Do them in one sitting or spread across a few — nothing expires and nothing is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Test Three Predictions About Model Behaviour
description: Use the mechanism from this module to predict, in writing, how a real model will behave in three situations you choose — then actually run them and confront what you got wrong.

learningObjectives.text: Generate falsifiable predictions about model behaviour from the prediction mechanism
Evaluate the gap between a mechanistic prediction and observed model behaviour

contentSections.body: You now have a mechanism that makes real, checkable predictions: fabrication risk should climb with obscurity and precision; letter/word-level tasks should be less reliable than token-level ones; well-covered topics should generalize cleanly even into novel phrasing. This lab asks you to bet on that, in writing, before you find out if you're right — the whole point of predicting before instruction, run on yourself this time.

contentSections.title: Three predictions, tested
contentSections.brief: You have access to any chat-based language model (a free tier is enough — this doesn't need a premium subscription). Using what this module covered — tokenization, fabrication risk, the limits of what "knowing" means for a model — write down three specific, falsifiable predictions about how it will behave, *before* you run anything. Then run them, and write down honestly what you got wrong.
contentSections.deliverable: A short document with three predictions (written before testing), the actual model outputs, and a plain-language account of what surprised you and why, tied back to the mechanism.

stages.title: Write three predictions, cold
stages.instructions: Before opening any AI tool, write three specific predictions about how a model will behave. They must be falsifiable — "it will get this wrong" or "it will answer confidently but incorrectly" or "it will hedge here," not vague guesses. Draw at least one from tokenization (a counting or letter-level task), at least one from fabrication risk (an obscure, precise question you can independently verify), and at least one of your own choosing from anywhere else in the module. Write each prediction as: the exact prompt you'll use, what you predict will happen, and why — citing the mechanism, not a hunch.
stages.checkpoint: You have three prompts written down with a specific predicted outcome and a stated mechanism-based reason for each, saved somewhere you won't edit after the fact.

stages.title: Run all three, unedited
stages.instructions: Run the exact three prompts you wrote, in a fresh conversation each (don't reuse context between them — that would change what you're testing). Copy the model's actual output for each, in full, without cleaning it up. If a prediction requires independent verification (a fact you can check), check it now and note whether the model was right.
stages.checkpoint: You have all three raw outputs saved, plus a verified true/false for any factual claim you predicted might be fabricated.

stages.title: Confront what you got wrong
stages.instructions: For each of the three, write a short honest verdict: did the outcome match your prediction? If it didn't, don't just note the mismatch — explain, using the mechanism, why your prediction was wrong. (If you were surprised the model did *better* than predicted, that's just as worth explaining as being surprised it did worse — both are data about where your mental model of the mechanism needs adjusting.) Close with one sentence: what would you predict differently next time?
stages.checkpoint: Each of the three predictions has a verdict and a mechanism-based explanation for any gap, and you have one closing sentence about what you'd adjust.

rubric.criterion: Predictions were written before testing, not adjusted afterward
rubric.meets: The three predictions and their stated reasons are visibly separate from, and written before, the actual outputs — no editing predictions to match what happened.

rubric.criterion: Predictions are genuinely falsifiable
rubric.meets: Each prediction names a specific, checkable outcome (right/wrong, hedges/doesn't, specific error type) rather than something too vague to be wrong about.

rubric.criterion: At least one prediction from tokenization and one from fabrication risk
rubric.meets: The three predictions visibly draw on at least two distinct mechanisms from the module, not three variations on the same idea.

rubric.criterion: Gaps are explained with the mechanism, not just noted
rubric.meets: Where a prediction didn't match, the explanation names *why*, in terms of training signal, tokenization, or the specific mechanism involved — not just 'I was wrong.'

rubric.criterion: Verification is real, not assumed
rubric.meets: Any factual claim the model made that was predicted to be risky was actually checked against an independent source, with the result recorded.

rubric.criterion: The closing adjustment is specific
rubric.meets: The final sentence names something concrete you'd predict differently, not a general statement like 'I'll be more careful.'

contentSections.body: Being wrong about a prediction and being able to say exactly why, mechanistically, is worth more than being right by luck — that's the actual skill this lab is testing.

title: Checkpoint — Prediction, Not Thinking
description: Ten questions pulling from this module. Ungraded, untimed — this is the first module in the phase, so every question draws on it; later checkpoints reach further back.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve the module's core mechanism and its consequences without looking them up

questions.from: This module — Prediction, Not Thinking
questions.prompt: In one sentence, what does a language model do to produce each token of its output?

options.label: Computes a probability distribution over the next token given everything so far, and samples one
Looks up the most relevant fact in a stored knowledge base
Plans the full response, then writes it out word by word

questions.explanation: That's the entire mechanism, repeated once per token, with the model's own prior output feeding back in as part of the input to the next step.

questions.from: This module — Prediction, Not Thinking
questions.prompt: What does "autoregressive" mean in this context?

options.label: The model's own previously generated tokens become part of the input for predicting the next one
The model automatically corrects its own grammar
The model regresses toward shorter answers over a long conversation

questions.explanation: It's the feedback loop: token five is predicted using the prompt plus tokens one through four, which the model itself just wrote.

questions.from: This module — Prediction, Not Thinking
questions.prompt: A model gets small multiplications right more often than very large ones. What does this pattern of degradation (graceful, not a hard cliff) suggest?

options.label: It's calculating internally but has a bug in large numbers
It's pattern-matching from training data shaped like arithmetic, which generalizes well to familiar-looking problems and worse to unfamiliar ones
It's answering randomly and short numbers happen to be right more often

questions.explanation: A true calculator fails catastrophically (wrong or overflow); a predictor fails gracefully, getting closer to right on more familiar-shaped problems — the graceful curve is itself evidence of pattern generalization, not real computation.

questions.from: This module — Prediction, Not Thinking
questions.prompt: Why does asking a model to reverse the letters in an uncommon word tend to go badly?

options.label: The model isn't trained on that specific word
The word is split into a small number of multi-letter tokens, and the model doesn't directly operate on individual characters
Reversal tasks require more computation than the model can perform

questions.explanation: The model's unit of operation is the token, not the letter — reconstructing exact character-level detail inside a token has to be inferred, not read off directly, which is why it's unreliable.

questions.from: This module — Prediction, Not Thinking
questions.prompt: Why can a model produce a fabricated citation that's formatted exactly like a real one?

options.label: It deliberately copies the format to deceive
Producing correct-looking form and verifying real-world existence are separate capabilities, and the model only has the first one
It's using an outdated version of a real database

questions.explanation: Citation *shape* is a well-supported text pattern the model learned thoroughly; whether a specific case *exists* is a fact about the world with no built-in verification step attached to the generation process.

questions.from: This module — Prediction, Not Thinking
questions.prompt: Which kind of question carries the highest fabrication risk?

options.label: A general, well-known fact stated approximately
An obscure topic combined with a request for an exact, precise detail
Any question phrased as a full sentence rather than a fragment

questions.explanation: Obscurity means thin, inconsistent training signal; precision removes any safe middle ground between exactly right and fabricated. Together they're close to a worst case.

questions.from: This module — Prediction, Not Thinking
questions.prompt: Someone says "it doesn't know anything, it's just statistics" to dismiss a model's chemistry explanation. What's the overreach in that statement?

options.label: There's no overreach — the statement is entirely accurate
"No verified fact-store" doesn't mean "no useful accurate structure" — strong, consistent training signal genuinely produces reliable output on well-covered topics
The model does have a verified fact-store, so the statement is simply false

questions.explanation: The absence of a checked, sourced knowledge base is real. But that doesn't mean the learned statistical structure isn't genuinely useful and often accurate — the two claims get conflated constantly.

questions.from: This module — Prediction, Not Thinking
questions.prompt: What's the accurate critique of "it's basically a search engine"?

options.label: Search engines are outdated technology
It wrongly implies retrieval of a real, traceable, checkable source — the model generates text with no guaranteed source behind any given claim
Search engines can't answer questions in full sentences

questions.explanation: A search engine retrieves an existing, checkable document. A model generates new token sequences from learned patterns — there's no retrieval step, which is exactly why a self-reported "source" can be fabricated.

questions.from: This module — Prediction, Not Thinking
questions.prompt: Why does a model's confident tone not tell you whether a specific claim is accurate?

options.label: Confidence and fluency are produced by the same process regardless of whether the content happens to be accurate — nothing couples tone to truth
The model deliberately hides its confidence level from users
Confidence only applies to short answers, not long ones

questions.explanation: Tone and structure are learned patterns like anything else; nothing in the mechanism forces confident phrasing to correlate with the underlying claim being checked or true.
