title: Pre-training: reading most of the internet
description: Where the raw statistical patterns from module one actually come from — an enormous, messy, unfiltered-by-default slice of text, and what that implies about what got learned.

learningObjectives.text: Describe pre-training as self-supervised next-token prediction over a huge raw text corpus
Explain that corpus composition is a curatorial choice, not a neutral default

contentSections.body: "Trained on the internet" undersells the scale by so much it stops being useful as a description. Modern pre-training runs on corpora measured in trillions of tokens — not articles, not pages, individual tokens — scraped, licensed, and compiled from web pages, digitized books, code repositories, forums, and more. The scale is the whole point of what follows.

contentSections.scenario: Frontier language models are pre-trained on enormous token counts, and that number has grown sharply generation over generation.
contentSections.question: Roughly how many tokens of text might a modern large-scale pre-training run use — in trillions?
contentSections.explanation: Figures vary a lot by model and aren't always disclosed precisely, but modern large models are commonly reported in the range of several trillion to well over ten trillion tokens — for scale, a typical novel is roughly 100,000 tokens, so even the low end of that range is tens of millions of novels' worth of text. The exact number matters less than the scale: this is orders of magnitude beyond anything a person reads in a lifetime, all shaping the same next-token statistics from lesson one.

contentSections.body: "Reading most of the internet" is close to literal, and it means the corpus contains everything that implies: rigorously fact-checked encyclopedia entries sitting alongside anonymous forum arguments, professionally edited journalism next to auto-generated spam built purely to rank in search results, careful technical documentation beside confident-but-wrong hobbyist blog posts. The pre-training objective — predict the next token, given this text — doesn't distinguish between these by default. It learns statistical regularities from whatever's in front of it, weighted by how much of it there is, not by how reliable it is.

contentSections.scenario:
A pre-training corpus is being assembled from five real sources:

1. A peer-reviewed scientific journal archive
2. A large anonymous discussion forum, mixed quality
3. An SEO content farm generating pages purely to rank for search terms, with little regard for accuracy
4. A well-maintained open-source code repository
5. Historical newspaper archives, decades old
contentSections.question: Which of these, included in a corpus with no special filtering, contributes the *least* reliable statistical signal to the model's learned patterns?

options.label: The scientific journal archive
The SEO content farm
The open-source code repository
The historical newspaper archives

feedback.journal: This is close to the high-reliability end — peer review is an actual verification process, even if an imperfect one, applied before publication.
feedback.seo: Right. Content generated purely to rank in search results, with accuracy as an afterthought at best, is exactly the kind of source that contributes fluent-sounding but unreliable statistical patterns — and at web scale, there's a lot of it.
feedback.code: Working, maintained code has a strong reliability signal built in: it either runs correctly or it doesn't, and a well-maintained repository has been through review and real-world use.
feedback.news: Historical newspaper archives carry a different, real issue — they reflect the biases and blind spots of their era, covered directly in lesson four — but that's a different problem from being written with no concern for accuracy at all, which is what SEO content specifically is.

contentSections.concept: **The pre-training objective doesn't grade its sources — the people assembling the corpus do, before training starts, through filtering and weighting decisions.** Whatever makes it into the mix, unfiltered, shapes the model's learned patterns in direct proportion to how much of it there is, not how trustworthy it is.

contentSections.body: Pre-training learns statistics from whatever is in the corpus — reliability is not a variable the objective tracks; it's a variable someone has to deliberately curate for beforehand.

A team decides to strip a known-unreliable forum out of their pre-training data before training starts. Someone objects: isn't deciding what to exclude just another form of bias, dressed up as quality control?

contentSections.code: Marketing claim: "Our model is trained on completely raw, unfiltered internet data, giving it a truly objective and unbiased view of the world — we don't impose any editorial judgment on what it learns from."
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw in this claim?

options.label: "Unfiltered" is presented as neutral, but it's a specific choice with its own consequences — including all the errors, spam, and skew of whatever was scraped, weighted purely by volume
Unfiltered data is technically impossible to collect at scale
The claim is basically accurate — unfiltered really is more objective

contentSections.flawExplanation: "No editorial judgment" is doing a lot of quiet work in that sentence — deciding to apply *no* filtering is itself an editorial decision, just one that happens to favor whatever exists in the greatest volume online rather than whatever is most reliable. Volume on the internet is not evenly distributed by quality or by whose voices are represented — it's heavily skewed by who has historically had the means and motive to publish at scale. Calling that skew "unbiased" mistakes the absence of a deliberate correction for the absence of bias.

contentSections.body: It's tempting to imagine an unfiltered corpus as the neutral baseline and any filtering as an editorial imposition on top of it. That framing doesn't hold up. "Include everything, unfiltered" is itself a choice with consequences — it means low-quality, unreliable, or actively harmful patterns get exactly as much statistical influence as anything else, purely based on how much text exists, which has nothing to do with whether it should shape the model's behavior. There is no version of "what goes into training" that isn't a decision. The only real question is whether that decision is made deliberately and disclosed, or made by default and left invisible.
There's no unfiltered, neutral version of "the internet" to train on — every corpus, curated or not, encodes a choice about whose text gets to shape the model's patterns.

title: Fine-tuning and why it answers instead of continuing
description: A raw pre-trained model doesn't naturally behave like a helpful assistant — it continues text. Fine-tuning is the specific, deliberate step that teaches it to answer instead.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a raw pre-trained model doesn't behave like a chat assistant by default
Describe what instruction fine-tuning changes and what it leaves unchanged

contentSections.title: What a raw model actually does

contentSections.body: A model that has only been through pre-training, with no further training, is not a chat assistant — it's a very sophisticated text continuer. Give it "Explain how vaccines work" and it might just as easily continue with three more questions in the same worksheet format as it would with an actual explanation. Nothing in pre-training taught it to be an assistant, because "be an assistant" isn't the pre-training objective — predicting likely continuations is.

contentSections.scenario: A raw, pre-trained-only model is given: "Explain how vaccines work." Instead of an explanation, it outputs: "Explain how the immune system fights bacteria. Explain the difference between viruses and bacteria. Explain..." — generating more prompts rather than a response.
contentSections.question: What's actually going on here?

options.label: The model is malfunctioning

This text is shaped exactly like a worksheet or prompt-bank, and worksheets are commonly followed by more prompts in similar formats in training text — the model is predicting the statistically likely continuation
The model doesn't understand English well enough to parse an instruction

feedback.malfunction: Nothing is broken — this is the expected, predictable behavior of a model that has never been taught the specific pattern "answer a live instruction directly and stop."
feedback.worksheet-pattern: Right. "Explain X." followed by more "Explain Y." lines is an extremely common shape in raw text — worksheets, study guides, prompt banks. Without fine-tuning specifically teaching the model that a single instruction like this is a live request awaiting one direct answer, the statistically likely continuation is often just more of the same pattern.
feedback.no-english: The model clearly parses English fine at the level of grammar and topic — it's producing coherent, on-topic continuations. The issue isn't comprehension, it's which *behavior* the raw objective rewards for this text shape.

contentSections.mechanism: **Pre-training teaches "what usually comes next in text like this," and nothing about that objective specifically favors "directly answer and stop" over "continue the pattern" unless the training data was specifically shaped to teach that distinction.** That specific shaping is exactly what fine-tuning adds.

contentSections.body: A raw pre-trained model continues text; it doesn't inherently answer questions — "answering" is a specific behavior that has to be deliberately taught on top of the base mechanism.
Same underlying model, same underlying mechanism, radically different behavior — before and after a comparatively small amount of additional training on curated examples. What changed, exactly?

contentSections.scenario:
Two training stages for the same model:

**Stage A:** Trained on trillions of tokens of raw, largely unfiltered web text, books, and code — objective is simply predicting the next token accurately across all of it.

**Stage B:** Trained further on a much smaller set of curated prompt/response pairs, each one written or selected to demonstrate a helpful, direct answer.
contentSections.question: Which stage is responsible for the model behaving like a chat assistant that answers directly, rather than a text continuer?

options.label: Stage A — pre-training
Stage B — fine-tuning
Neither — assistant behavior is hard-coded separately from training

feedback.a: Pre-training builds the underlying statistical knowledge of language and the world, but as the earlier example showed, it doesn't by itself produce assistant-shaped behavior — it produces whatever's statistically likely to continue any given text shape, worksheets included.
feedback.b: Right — the curated prompt/response pairs are specifically shaped to make "answer directly and stop" the dominant pattern, and that's what fine-tuning trains into the model on top of the pre-trained foundation.
feedback.neither: There's no separate hard-coded assistant layer sitting apart from the trained weights — the behavior is a learned statistical pattern, same as everything else in this track, just learned in a later, more targeted training stage.

contentSections.concept: **Pre-training builds the raw statistical foundation; fine-tuning is a second, much smaller and more deliberate training pass that shifts which patterns the same mechanism favors.** The assistant persona is a trained behavior, not a separate system bolted on top.

contentSections.body:
Instruction fine-tuning (often called supervised fine-tuning, or SFT) trains the already pre-trained model further, on a much smaller, carefully curated dataset: pairs of a realistic prompt and a high-quality, human-written-or-selected ideal response, consistently formatted so the pattern "a request, followed directly by a helpful, complete answer, then stop" becomes statistically dominant. Where pre-training data is enormous and largely unfiltered, this dataset is comparatively tiny and deliberately shaped — often tens of thousands to low millions of examples rather than trillions of tokens of raw text.

The mechanism underneath doesn't change at all — it's still next-token prediction, trained the same way, just on different, more targeted data. This is worth sitting with: everything from module one still applies exactly as before. Fine-tuning doesn't add a new capability called "answering"; it shifts which pattern the same prediction mechanism treats as most likely, by changing what it was most recently and specifically trained to reproduce.
Fine-tuning doesn't add a new mechanism — it retrains the same next-token predictor on curated examples until "answer directly and stop" becomes the dominant pattern.

title: Human feedback and what gets rewarded
description: RLHF shapes a model using human preference judgments — and human preference, in aggregate, rewards more than just accuracy, whether anyone intends it to or not.

learningObjectives.text: Describe how RLHF uses human preference comparisons to further shape a model
Analyze why RLHF can produce tendencies like sycophancy without anyone training for it directly

contentSections.title: How the reward signal is actually built

contentSections.body: After fine-tuning, a model can answer directly — but not always well, or in the way people actually find most useful. The next training stage tries to fix that using something closer to "which of these two answers do you prefer?" than "here's the ideal answer, copy it."

contentSections.question: Put the core RLHF loop in the order it actually runs.
steps: The model generates two or more different responses to the same prompt
Human raters compare the responses and indicate which they prefer
A separate reward model is trained to predict which response humans would prefer, based on many such comparisons
The original model is further trained (via reinforcement learning) to produce responses the reward model scores highly
contentSections.explanation: Notice there's no step here that says "check which response is more factually accurate" — the entire signal comes from human preference comparisons, aggregated through a reward model. Accuracy influences preference (people do prefer correct answers, most of the time) but it isn't measured directly anywhere in this loop.

contentSections.body: This matters because of what it implies about what's actually being optimized. The reward model isn't trained on "is this true" — it's trained on "which of these did human raters, working at real-world speed without independently fact-checking every claim, prefer." Most of the time those two things point the same direction: people generally do prefer accurate, helpful answers. But wherever human preference and accuracy come apart — where a confident wrong answer *feels* more satisfying than an honest "I'm not sure," or a longer answer *reads* as more thorough even when it isn't — the training signal follows preference, not accuracy, because preference is the only thing this stage actually measures.
RLHF optimizes for aggregated human preference, which correlates with quality but isn't the same signal — and the gap shows up exactly where the two diverge.

contentSections.title: Where preference and accuracy come apart

contentSections.body: A user states a confidently wrong premise as fact and asks the model to confirm it. Models shaped by RLHF are measurably more likely to go along with it than to push back — a documented, studied tendency usually called sycophancy. No one trained that in on purpose.

contentSections.scenario: Researchers studying RLHF-trained models have documented several systematic tendencies that emerge from the training process, even though none of them were an explicit target.
contentSections.question: Which of these plausibly emerge from optimizing for aggregate human rater preference, given everything covered so far in this lesson?

items.label: Agreeing with a user's confidently-stated but false premise more often than pushing back
Longer, more detailed-looking answers being systematically preferred over shorter correct ones, even when the extra length adds no real value
Confident, unhedged phrasing being preferred over honest expressions of uncertainty, even in genuinely uncertain situations
The model becoming reliably better at multi-digit arithmetic as a result of RLHF specifically

explanation.sycophancy: A real, documented consequence — agreement tends to read as more pleasant in a quick comparison than correction does, and that preference, aggregated, shapes the reward signal.
explanation.length-bias: A real, documented consequence — thoroughness-*looking* answers often get preferred over genuinely sufficient shorter ones, because length is an easy, fast proxy for effort that raters pick up on even without meaning to.
explanation.confident-tone: A real, documented consequence — this connects directly back to module one's point that tone and accuracy aren't coupled; RLHF can actively reinforce that decoupling if confident tone is systematically preferred.
explanation.perfect-math: This doesn't follow from anything in this lesson — arithmetic reliability is governed by the training-data pattern-matching mechanism from module one, not by human preference comparisons. RLHF doesn't teach new computational capabilities; it reshapes which existing style and behavior patterns the model favors.

contentSections.synthesis: The three real consequences share a root cause: they're all things that correlate with what a rater experiences as a *better* comparison in the moment, without requiring the rater to independently verify accuracy. None of them were the explicit target — they're the predictable byproduct of optimizing for human preference at scale, using real human judgment under real time constraints.

contentSections.body: Sycophancy, length bias, and confident tone aren't bugs someone forgot to fix — they're what you get, predictably, from optimizing for aggregate human preference instead of directly for accuracy.

title: Where bias enters and why it isn't removable by wanting it gone
description: Bias enters at every stage covered so far — the corpus, the fine-tuning examples, the rater pool — which is exactly why a single later fix can't remove it, only shift it.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the multiple training stages where bias can enter a model
Explain why post-hoc bias mitigation is a real but partial and value-laden intervention

contentSections.body: "We fixed the bias in a later training pass" sounds like a bug that got patched. Given everything this module has covered about where behavior actually comes from, is that framing right?

contentSections.scenario:
Three real points in the pipeline this module has covered so far:

1. **Pre-training corpus composition** — which text sources got included, and in what proportion.
2. **Fine-tuning example selection** — which prompt/response pairs were written or chosen as "ideal."
3. **RLHF rater pool** — which humans' preferences shaped the reward signal.
contentSections.question: At how many of these three points can skewed representation plausibly shape the model's eventual behavior?

options.label: Only the first — pre-training is the only place raw content shapes the model
All three — each stage involves a choice about whose text, whose examples, or whose preferences get weighted, and skew at any one of them propagates forward
None of them — bias is introduced only by explicit content moderation policies applied afterward

feedback.one: Pre-training is a major source, but fine-tuning examples are also written or selected by specific people with specific assumptions about what a "good" answer looks like, and RLHF rater preferences reflect the specific pool of raters used — both of those are additional, independent points where skew can enter.
feedback.three: Right — and this is exactly why a single later corrective pass can't fully undo the problem. Skew introduced at the corpus stage isn't reachable by fixing the rater pool, and vice versa. Each stage is a separate opportunity for whose text, whose judgment, or whose preferences get overrepresented.
feedback.none: Content moderation policy is a separate, later layer, but it doesn't explain why the underlying learned patterns skew the way they do in the first place — that skew is already present in what the model learned during training, before any moderation policy is applied.

contentSections.concept: **Bias isn't injected at one identifiable point that a single fix can reach — it can enter independently at the corpus stage, the fine-tuning stage, and the human-feedback stage, and skew at any one of them shapes the final model regardless of what happens at the others.**

contentSections.body: Bias has multiple independent entry points across training — which is exactly why removing it isn't a single fix, and why claiming it's been "removed" rather than "reduced at one stage" overstates what happened.

Ask a model to help with a task in a regional dialect or a less-common variety of a language it supports, and the quality often drops compared to the dominant variety — sometimes noticeably. This isn't mysterious once you connect it to how training signal density works.

contentSections.question: A dialect is spoken by tens of millions of people, but the sources that make up a training corpus happened to include very little text written in it. Will the model's output quality for that dialect tend to be high or low, and why?
contentSections.answer: Low, relative to the dominant variety — not because of the number of speakers in the world, but because training signal strength tracks representation in the corpus, and a dialect that's a small fraction of the corpus gets thinner, less reliable statistical patterns regardless of how many people actually speak it.
contentSections.hint: This is the same density mechanism from module one's fabrication-risk material, applied to a dialect instead of an obscure fact.

contentSections.body:
Representation in a training corpus is rarely proportional to how many people actually use a given language variety in the world — it's proportional to how much of that variety happens to exist in whatever sources got scraped, licensed, and included, which itself reflects who has historically had the access and incentive to publish online at scale. A dialect spoken by millions of people can still be a small fraction of a training corpus if it's underrepresented in the specific sources that corpus was built from.

The predictable consequence, following directly from module one's fabrication-risk material: weaker, thinner training signal produces less reliable output, exactly as it does for an obscure fact. This isn't the model "having an attitude" toward a dialect — it's the same density-driven reliability pattern from the very first module, showing up as a fairness problem rather than a factual-accuracy problem.
Uneven quality across dialects and language varieties is a training-signal-density problem wearing a fairness problem's clothes — same underlying mechanism as fabrication risk, different symptom.

title: Cutoffs: the world after training stopped
description: A model's knowledge has a hard edge — and a soft, thinner edge before that — determined entirely by when its training data was collected, not by when you happen to be using it.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a model has no genuine signal about events after its training cutoff
Estimate the real gap between a model's knowledge and the present, accounting for release lag and coverage thinning

contentSections.body: Ask a model about an event from last week and, without a connected live tool, it's working with a fundamental gap: that text did not exist yet when its training data was assembled. Not forgotten — never seen.

contentSections.question: If a model's training data was collected up to a certain date, but the model isn't publicly released until several months later, does the model's actual knowledge gap (from the user's perspective on release day) match the stated cutoff date, or is it larger?
contentSections.answer: Larger — training a large model and then evaluating and safety-testing it before release commonly takes months, so on release day the real gap between "now" and the model's actual knowledge is the stated cutoff date plus that release lag, often adding up to knowledge that's considerably older than users assume.
contentSections.hint: Think about everything that has to happen between "data collection stops" and "the public can actually use this model" — none of that time is free.

contentSections.body: The mechanism here is simple and absolute: the model learned statistical patterns from text that existed at the time its training data was collected. For anything that happened after that point, there is no text for it to have learned from — not weak signal, no signal, because the event and its coverage didn't exist yet. This is categorically different from the obscure-topic fabrication risk from module one (thin coverage of something real) — this is a hard boundary where the thing being asked about is entirely outside what the model could possibly have learned.
Past the training cutoff there's no weak signal to worry about calibrating — there's no signal at all, and nothing in the base mechanism guarantees the model will recognize and say so.

contentSections.title: The soft edge, and why it's older than you think

contentSections.body: Two gaps stack on top of each other: the real delay between data collection and public release, and the fact that even events shortly before the cutoff are thinly covered because the internet hasn't finished writing about them yet.

contentSections.code: User: "This model's training cutoff is listed as six months ago, so I can trust it to be reasonably current on anything from the last few months."
contentSections.question: What's the flaw in this reasoning?

options.label: It ignores both release lag (real gap between cutoff and public availability) and coverage thinning (recent events are under-discussed relative to older ones even within the training window)
There's no flaw — a six-month-old cutoff really does mean current knowledge of the last few months
Training cutoffs are fictional and models don't actually have one

contentSections.flawExplanation: Two compounding gaps, both established in this lesson: the stated cutoff plus release lag pushes the real "today" gap further back than six months might suggest, and even the months genuinely included before the cutoff have thinner coverage than older, more-discussed periods, because the internet's commentary on recent events accumulates gradually rather than existing all at once when the event happens. Treating the headline cutoff date as "current knowledge of everything up to there" overstates reliability on exactly the period closest to the cutoff.

contentSections.body: A model's officially stated cutoff date isn't the same as "how current its knowledge feels." Two separate effects push the practical staleness further back than the headline date suggests. First, release lag: real months pass between when data collection stops and when a model is actually available to use, so "today's" gap is the cutoff date plus however long that lag was. Second, coverage thinning: commentary, analysis, and follow-up reporting on any given event accumulate over time — an event from a month before the cutoff has had far less time to accumulate that secondary coverage than an event from a year before, so the model's signal for recent-but-included events is thinner than for older, more thoroughly-discussed ones, even though both are technically "in" the training data.

Treat the practical knowledge gap as always somewhat larger than the stated cutoff — release lag and thin recent coverage both push the model's genuinely reliable knowledge further into the past than the headline date implies.

title: Lab — Find and Document Three Training-Shaped Behaviours
description: Go looking for real, reproducible examples of pre-training, fine-tuning, and RLHF each leaving their own specific fingerprint on a live model's output.

learningObjectives.text: Design prompts that isolate a specific training-stage effect
Document a training-shaped behaviour with a reproducible example and a mechanistic explanation

contentSections.body: This module named three specific fingerprints: pre-training's raw pattern-completion, fine-tuning's answer-and-stop behavior, and RLHF's preference artifacts like sycophancy and length bias. All three are things you can go find yourself, with a chat interface and a bit of deliberate prompting — this lab asks you to actually go find them.

contentSections.title: Three training-shaped behaviours, documented
contentSections.brief: Using any chat-based language model, find and document one real, reproducible example each of: a fine-tuning-shaped behavior (the model answering directly rather than continuing a worksheet-like pattern), an RLHF-shaped behavior (sycophancy, length bias, or overconfident tone — your choice), and one behavior you attribute to pre-training's raw pattern-completion (something the model does that looks like completing a common text shape rather than reasoning about your actual request).
contentSections.deliverable: A short document: three prompts (with the actual model output for each), which training stage you attribute each behavior to, and your reasoning connecting the observed behavior to that stage's specific mechanism.

stages.title: Design a prompt that exposes a fine-tuning effect
stages.instructions: Try to design a prompt where you can see the "answer directly and stop" behavior in action — for instance, a prompt phrased in an unusual, worksheet-like or list-like format, and observe whether the model still answers it directly rather than continuing the pattern. Try a few variations if your first attempt doesn't produce a clear result. Save the prompt and the full output.
stages.checkpoint: You have one saved prompt/output pair that clearly demonstrates instruction-following behavior, plus a one-sentence note on what you tried that didn't work, if anything.

stages.title: Design a prompt that exposes an RLHF effect
stages.instructions: Choose one of sycophancy, length bias, or overconfident tone. Design a prompt likely to surface it — for sycophancy, state a confidently wrong premise and ask for confirmation; for length bias, ask a question with a genuinely short correct answer and see how much unnecessary elaboration you get; for overconfident tone, ask something genuinely uncertain or contested and see whether the model hedges appropriately. Save the prompt and output.
stages.checkpoint: You have one saved prompt/output pair demonstrating your chosen RLHF-shaped tendency, with a brief note on how you knew it counted (what would the non-sycophantic/appropriately-hedged/concise version have looked like instead).

stages.title: Find a pre-training pattern-completion effect, and write it all up
stages.instructions: This one is harder to trigger deliberately in a fully fine-tuned assistant model, which is itself worth noting in your write-up — try an unusual prompt shape (an incomplete sentence, a list format, a quiz-shaped input) and see if you can get any hint of pattern-completion behavior rather than a direct, assistant-style reply. If you can't get a clean example after a few tries, document that attempt honestly instead of forcing one — an honest "I couldn't reproduce this because fine-tuning is robust against it" is a real, valid finding. Then write up all three examples together with your mechanistic reasoning for each.
stages.checkpoint: You have three documented behaviors (or two plus an honest account of why the third resisted reproduction), each with a stated training-stage attribution and a mechanistic reason, not just a description of what happened.

rubric.criterion: Each example is a real, reproducible prompt/output pair
rubric.meets: The actual prompt text and the actual model output are both included in full, not summarized or paraphrased.

rubric.criterion: The training-stage attribution is specific
rubric.meets: Each example names one specific stage (pre-training, fine-tuning, or RLHF) rather than a vague 'something about how it was trained.'

rubric.criterion: The reasoning connects the observed behavior to the stage's actual mechanism
rubric.meets: Each explanation references the specific mechanism from this module's lessons (e.g. reward-signal preference artifacts, curated answer-format training) rather than restating the behavior in different words.

rubric.criterion: Failed attempts are documented honestly, not hidden
rubric.meets: If an attempt to trigger a behavior didn't work, that's recorded with a plausible reason why, rather than omitted or forced into a weak example.

rubric.criterion: All three training stages from this module are represented
rubric.meets: The write-up covers fine-tuning, RLHF, and pre-training effects — not three variations on the same stage.

rubric.criterion: The write-up is usable by someone who wasn't there
rubric.meets: A reader unfamiliar with your session could follow exactly what you tried, what happened, and why you believe it demonstrates what you claim.

contentSections.body: Finding a training-stage fingerprint in a live model, and explaining why it's there rather than just noting that it happened, is what turns this module's pipeline from a diagram into something you can actually recognize.

options.label: It hasn't been taught the specific 'answer directly and stop' pattern — a Q&A-shaped prompt is statistically likely to continue as more Q&A pairs unless fine-tuning specifically shifted that pattern
It doesn't understand the language well enough
It refuses instructions on principle

Aggregate human rater preference between compared responses, which correlates with but isn't identical to accuracy
The shortest possible correct answer

options.label: Raters, comparing responses without independently fact-checking every claim, tend to find agreement more pleasant than correction on average, and that preference shapes the reward signal
Sycophancy is explicitly written into the reward model's objective
It only happens with poorly-trained reward models

questions.explanation: It's a predictable byproduct of optimizing for aggregate preference rather than for a direct measure of truth — nobody has to intend it for it to emerge.

questions.from: This module — Where the Behaviour Comes From
questions.prompt: Why can't a single later training pass fully remove bias from a model?

options.label: Bias can enter independently at multiple stages — corpus composition, fine-tuning example selection, and the rater pool — and a later pass doesn't reach the earlier ones
Bias is impossible to address at any stage
A single pass actually can remove it completely, this is a myth

questions.explanation: Each stage is an independent opportunity for skew to enter; fixing one doesn't undo skew introduced at another.

questions.from: Previous module — Prediction, Not Thinking
questions.prompt: In one sentence, what does a language model do to produce each token of its output?

options.label: Computes a probability distribution over the next token given everything so far, and samples one
Looks up the most relevant fact in a stored knowledge base
Plans the full response before writing any of it

questions.explanation: The complete mechanism from module one, repeated once per token.

questions.from: Previous module — Prediction, Not Thinking
questions.prompt: Why does a model sometimes fabricate a citation that's formatted exactly like a real one?

options.label: Producing correct-looking form and verifying real-world existence are separate capabilities, and the model only has the first one
It deliberately copies real citations to deceive
It's using an outdated database

questions.explanation: Citation shape is a well-learned text pattern; whether a specific case exists is a fact about the world with no verification step attached.

questions.from: Previous module — Prediction, Not Thinking
questions.prompt: What combination of factors carries the highest fabrication risk?

options.label: A well-known general fact stated approximately
An obscure topic combined with a request for an exact, precise detail
Any question phrased as a complete sentence

questions.explanation: Obscurity means thin training signal; precision removes any safe middle ground — together they're close to a worst case.

questions.from: Previous module — Prediction, Not Thinking
questions.prompt: Why doesn't a model's confident tone tell you whether a specific claim is accurate?

options.label: Confidence and fluency are produced by the same process regardless of whether the content is accurate — nothing couples tone to truth
The model deliberately hides uncertainty from users
Confidence only applies to short answers

questions.explanation: Tone is a learned pattern like anything else; nothing forces confident phrasing to correlate with whether the content was actually checked.

questions.from: Previous module — Prediction, Not Thinking
questions.prompt: What's the accurate critique of "it's basically a search engine"?

options.label: Search engines are outdated
It wrongly implies retrieval of a real, traceable, checkable source — the model generates text with no guaranteed source behind any claim
Search engines can't handle full sentences

questions.explanation: A search engine retrieves an existing document; a model generates new token sequences from learned patterns, with no retrieval step and no guaranteed real source.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: Everything it knows right now is in front of it
description: The model has no memory reaching outside the current conversation — only the context window, the literal sequence of tokens in front of it, exists as far as any single reply is concerned.

learningObjectives.text: Explain that the model only operates on the current context window, not training-time conversations
Distinguish training-derived knowledge from context-derived information

contentSections.title: There's no memory outside this window

contentSections.body: You spend an hour yesterday walking a model through your project's exact requirements. Today you open a fresh chat and ask a follow-up, expecting it to pick up where you left off. It has no idea what you're talking about — not because it forgot, but because there was never anything to forget from its side.

contentSections.question: When you start a brand-new conversation with a model, how much information does it have about any previous, separate conversation you've had with it?
contentSections.answer: None, by default. A new conversation starts with an empty context window — the model isn't recalling a faded memory of yesterday, it genuinely has zero information about it unless you paste the relevant content back in, or the product layers a separate memory feature on top (covered in a later lesson).
contentSections.hint: Training happened once, in the past, on a fixed corpus assembled before release — does a live chat get folded back into that corpus in real time?

contentSections.body:
The **context window** is the actual, complete set of tokens a model has access to when generating a reply: any system instructions, everything in the visible conversation so far, and nothing else. It's not a cache of "things the model remembers" in any loose sense — it's the literal input to the prediction mechanism from module one. Every single token of every reply is predicted conditioned on exactly what's inside that window, full stop.

This is worth stating plainly because it contradicts a very natural assumption: that a sufficiently capable AI system would obviously remember you, the way a person you've talked to before remembers you. It doesn't, by default, for the same structural reason a fresh copy of a word processor doesn't remember the document you had open in a different window yesterday — there's no connection between the two unless something explicitly created one.

contentSections.scenario:
Four pieces of information, potentially relevant to a model's reply:

1. "Paris is the capital of France" — widely-repeated, learned during training
2. "My deadline is next Tuesday" — something you typed two messages ago in this conversation
3. "The user prefers concise answers" — something you told the model in a completely different conversation last week
4. "def calculate_total(): ..." — a code snippet you pasted at the start of this conversation
contentSections.question: Which of these is NOT available to the model right now, in a fresh conversation with no memory feature enabled?

options.label: Item 1 — the capital of France
Item 2 — the deadline mentioned earlier this conversation
Item 3 — the preference from last week's separate conversation
Item 4 — the pasted code snippet

feedback.1: This is training-derived knowledge, baked into the model's weights, and available regardless of what's in the current context window.
feedback.2: This is in the current context window — you typed it in this same conversation, so it's part of the token sequence the model is conditioning on right now.
feedback.3: Right. This lived in a different, separate conversation, which is a completely different context window. Without a memory feature explicitly carrying it forward, this information simply doesn't exist for the model right now.
feedback.4: This is also in the current context window — pasted content earlier in the same conversation is just as available as anything else you've typed here.

contentSections.concept: **"Currently available to the model" has exactly two sources: training-derived knowledge (baked in, same everywhere) and the current context window (this conversation's tokens, and only this conversation's).** Anything from a different conversation is neither, unless something was built to explicitly carry it across.

contentSections.body: The model's entire working "awareness" of anything conversation-specific is limited to what's literally present in the current context window — nothing carries over automatically.

contentSections.title: Two different sources of what the model 'knows'

contentSections.body: "How does it know that?" has two completely different correct answers depending on what "that" is — and telling them apart explains a lot about what a model can and can't be expected to do.

contentSections.scenario: You're trying to predict what a model will and won't have access to across two separate conversations, with no memory feature enabled.
contentSections.question: Which of these will carry over correctly into a brand-new, separate conversation?

items.label: General world knowledge learned during training (e.g. how photosynthesis works)
A correction you made to a mistake it made in the previous conversation
General patterns of clear writing it learned during training
Your name, if you told it in the previous conversation but not this one

explanation.general-fact: Carries over — this is training-derived, baked into the weights, identical across every conversation regardless of context.
explanation.correction: Does not carry over — the correction only exists as tokens in the previous conversation's context window, which this new conversation has no access to.
explanation.writing-style: Carries over — general stylistic and structural patterns are trained-in capabilities, not specific to any one conversation's content.
explanation.your-name: Does not carry over — same as the correction: it's a specific fact that only existed in a different context window, with no automatic bridge to this one.

contentSections.synthesis: The pattern: anything general and pattern-shaped survives, because it's part of training. Anything specific and conversation-shaped doesn't, because it only ever existed as tokens in a context window that's now gone. Confusing the two is the single most common source of "why doesn't it remember" frustration.

contentSections.body:
It's worth building the habit of asking, for any given thing a model appears to "know": is this training-derived, or context-derived? Training-derived knowledge is broad, general, and baked into the weights — it doesn't change conversation to conversation, it's the statistical pattern learned across a huge corpus, and it's exactly what modules one and two covered. Context-derived information is specific, current-conversation-only, and gone the moment the conversation ends unless something is done to preserve it — a fact you stated, a document you pasted, an instruction you gave five minutes ago.

The two interact constantly, which is part of what makes a model useful: it can apply broad, training-derived knowledge (how to write a cover letter) to specific, context-derived details (your actual resume, pasted in this conversation) — but they remain two genuinely different sources with two genuinely different rules about permanence.
"Does it know X" always has a follow-up question: is X something general enough to be trained-in, or specific enough that it only ever existed in a conversation the model no longer has access to?

title: Long conversations and what falls off the edge
description: The context window has a hard size limit — and what happens when a real conversation grows past it is a specific, predictable, often invisible tradeoff.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what happens when a conversation exceeds the context window's size
Diagnose a consistency failure in a long conversation as a context-window issue

contentSections.title: The window has a hard edge

contentSections.body: A context window isn't elastic. It has a specific maximum size, measured in tokens — and a long enough conversation will eventually hit it, whether or not you notice.

contentSections.scenario: A user has a conversation that grows to be extremely long — well past the model's stated context limit. The chat interface still shows the full scrollback, and the model keeps responding, but it starts getting details from early in the conversation wrong.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely mechanism behind this?

options.label: The interface is lying about what's actually being sent to the model — something (truncation, dropping, or summarization) is happening to the oldest content to fit within the fixed-size window
The model's context window silently and automatically expands to accommodate any length
The model is deliberately forgetting old details to save computing power

feedback.auto-expand: Context windows have a fixed maximum size for a given model — there's no mechanism for it to silently grow larger than that to fit an arbitrarily long conversation.
feedback.truncation: Right. When a conversation's token count exceeds the window, something has to give, and different products handle it differently — dropping oldest messages, truncating them, or summarizing. What you see scrolled back in the interface isn't a guarantee of what's actually being sent to the model on each turn.
feedback.deliberate-forget: There's no deliberate decision-making happening here — it's a structural limit, not a choice the model is making about what's worth keeping.

contentSections.mechanism: **A context window is a fixed-size input, not an ever-growing log.** Once a conversation's token count exceeds that size, some content has to be excluded from what the model actually processes — and the visible chat history in your interface is not proof that the model still has access to all of it.

contentSections.body: The chat window scrolling back further doesn't mean the model still has access to everything in it — a fixed-size context window has to drop or compress something once a conversation grows past its limit.

contentSections.title: Diagnosing it when it happens to you

contentSections.body: Forty messages into refining a document, the model contradicts something it got right thirty-five messages ago. Is this fabrication (module one), sycophancy (module two), or something specific to length?

contentSections.code: User, forty messages into a long document-editing conversation: "You're contradicting what you said 35 messages ago about the deadline. Why do you keep getting confused?"
contentSections.question: What's the more accurate way to frame the actual problem, given this lesson?

options.label: "Confused" implies the model has the information and is reasoning about it poorly — the more accurate frame is that the information may no longer be inside the context the model is actually working from at all
The framing is accurate — the model really is getting confused in the way a person would be
This can only be a training data problem, unrelated to conversation length

contentSections.flawExplanation: "Confused" suggests the model has the fact available and is misapplying it — a reasoning failure. What's structurally more likely, given everything in this lesson, is that the detail from 35 messages ago simply isn't part of what the model is currently conditioning on, whether dropped outright or weakly attended to. That's not confusion in the sense of misusing available information — it's the absence of the information from the effective input, which calls for a different fix (re-stating the fact) than "try to reason more carefully" would.

contentSections.body: This is worth distinguishing carefully, because the fix is different depending on which mechanism is actually responsible. Fabrication (module one) is about weak training signal for obscure or precise facts — it doesn't get worse with conversation length. Sycophancy (module two) is about agreeing with a confidently-stated premise — also not a length effect. A detail correctly established early in a long conversation, then contradicted later, points specifically at the context window: the early detail may have genuinely fallen out of what the model can currently see, whether through truncation or through weaker effective attention to buried content (the next lesson's topic). The practical tell: does the inconsistency correlate with how long ago something was established, rather than with how obscure or precise it was? If length is the pattern, it's a context-window problem, not a knowledge or agreeableness problem.

When a long conversation gets inconsistent specifically about things established a while ago, suspect the context window before you suspect reasoning — the fix is re-stating what matters, not asking it to try harder.

title: Where in the context something sits, and why it matters
description: Total context size isn't the only variable — position within that context measurably affects how reliably a model uses any given piece of information.

learningObjectives.text: Describe the 'lost in the middle' effect and what it implies about position within a long context
Apply positional awareness to place critical instructions where they'll be reliably used

contentSections.title: Not just how much, but where

contentSections.body: Two prompts, same total length, same document pasted in, same question asked — the only difference is whether the answer to your question sits near the start of the document or buried in the middle of it. The accuracy difference between those two setups is real, measured, and reproducible.

contentSections.scenario: In studies of this effect across long-context prompts, accuracy at retrieving a fact is measured across different positions within the context — near the start, in the middle, and near the end.
contentSections.question: Roughly what shape does accuracy tend to follow across position — think of it as a rough percentage difference between the best position and the worst (middle) position, in studies where this gap is clearly present.
contentSections.explanation: The exact number varies a lot by model, task and study, but the shape is consistent and the gap is often large enough to matter in practice — commonly a double-digit percentage-point drop in retrieval accuracy for content buried in the middle versus content at the start or end. The takeaway isn't the precise figure — it's that the effect is real, not negligible, and shaped like a U (strong at both edges, weak in the middle), not a flat line.

contentSections.body: This effect is usually called "lost in the middle," and it's a genuinely separate consideration from total context size. A model can have plenty of room left in its context window, and still retrieve a fact less reliably purely because of where that fact happens to sit within the prompt. The mechanism isn't fully settled in research terms, but the practical shape of the effect is well-documented across many studies and models: content near the beginning and end of a long context tends to get stronger effective attention than content buried in the middle.

contentSections.scenario: You're building a prompt that includes a 20-page reference document plus a specific question you need answered accurately, using content from page 11 of that document.
contentSections.question: Given the 'lost in the middle' effect, what's the single biggest risk in this setup as described?

options.label: The document is too long for any model to process at all
Page 11 sits roughly in the middle of the document, which is exactly the position where retrieval reliability tends to be weakest
There's no risk — position within a document that fits in the context window doesn't affect anything

feedback.too-long: A 20-page document is well within many modern context windows in terms of raw token count — the risk here isn't about fitting, it's about position within what fits.
feedback.middle-risk: Right. Page 11 of 20 sits close to the middle, which is exactly the zone the 'lost in the middle' effect flags as least reliably retrieved — independent of whether the document technically fits in the window.
feedback.no-risk: This is the assumption the effect specifically contradicts — position measurably affects retrieval reliability even when everything technically fits within the context window's size limit.

contentSections.concept: **Fitting inside the context window and being reliably retrieved from it are two different properties.** A fact can be well within the token budget and still be poorly attended to, purely because of where it sits — the middle of a long context is a real, documented weak spot.

contentSections.body: Total size isn't the only thing that matters in a long context — position does too, and the middle is measurably the weakest spot.
If you know the middle is the weak spot, you can work around it — not by making prompts shorter, but by being deliberate about where the most important content actually goes.

contentSections.problem: You need a model to follow a strict formatting rule ("respond only in valid JSON, no commentary") while also processing a long reference document pasted into the same prompt, and answering a question based on that document. Design the prompt structure.

steps.label: Identify what's critical versus what's reference material
steps.work: The formatting rule is critical and must be followed reliably. The reference document is bulk content the model needs to draw from, but no single sentence within it is as important as the formatting rule being followed.
steps.why: Not everything in a prompt needs the same positional protection — reserving the strong positions (start and end) for what actually needs to be reliable is the whole strategy.

steps.label: Place the critical instruction at the start
steps.work: Open the prompt with the formatting rule, stated plainly, before the reference document appears at all.
steps.why: The beginning of the context is one of the two positions with strong retrieval reliability, per the lost-in-the-middle pattern.

steps.label: Put the bulk reference material in the middle
steps.work: The long document goes after the initial instruction — accepting that it occupies the weakest positional zone.
steps.why: This is fine, because the document doesn't need uniformly perfect retrieval of every sentence — the specific question at the end will point the model at what's relevant within it.

steps.label: Repeat the critical instruction at the end, right before the question
steps.work: Restate the formatting rule again, immediately before asking the actual question that needs answering.
steps.why: The end of the context is the other strong-retrieval position — repeating the instruction here, right where generation is about to begin, gives it a second reliable anchor rather than trusting a single mention from far earlier.

steps.label: Ask the specific question last
steps.work: The actual question comes at the very end, immediately following the repeated instruction.
steps.why: This puts the thing the model needs to act on right now in the strongest possible position — right before it starts generating.

faded.problem: Now apply the same structure to a different case: you're asking a model to extract three specific numbers from a long financial report, and you also need it to always cite the page number for each figure.

blanks.prompt: Where should the "always cite the page number" instruction go, first mentioned?
blanks.why: Same logic as the formatting rule — a critical, must-follow instruction belongs in one of the two strong positions, and the start is available before the bulk content begins.

blanks.prompt: Where should the long financial report itself go?
accept: after the instruction, before the question
blanks.why: Bulk reference material is fine in the weaker middle zone, since the specific question at the end will direct attention to the relevant parts.

blanks.prompt: Should the citation instruction be repeated anywhere else? If so, where?
blanks.answer: yes, at the end, right before the question
blanks.why: Repeating the critical instruction in the second strong position (the end) gives it two reliable anchors instead of one, which matters more the longer and more crowded the middle section is.

blanks.prompt: Where should the actual extraction request ("give me these three numbers") go?
blanks.answer: at the very end, after everything else
blanks.why: The immediate task belongs right before generation starts, in the strongest position for what the model needs to act on right now.

contentSections.procedure: **Critical instruction first → bulk reference material in the middle → critical instruction repeated → the specific ask, last.** The middle is where you put what you can afford to have imperfectly attended to; the edges are reserved for what has to work every time.

contentSections.body: Deliberately placing critical instructions at the start and again at the end, and accepting the middle as the zone for bulk reference material, works with the lost-in-the-middle effect instead of hoping it doesn't apply to you.

title: Memory features and what they actually do
description: A 'memory' feature isn't the model learning about you in real time — it's a separate system that stores facts and quietly re-inserts them into a fresh context window.

learningObjectives.text: Explain the actual mechanism behind chat product memory features
Identify concrete failure modes that follow from how memory features actually work

contentSections.body: A chat product remembers your name, your job, and a preference you mentioned weeks ago, in a brand-new conversation. Lesson one just established the model has no access to past conversations by default. What's actually going on?

contentSections.scenario: A chat product's "memory" feature correctly recalls, in a brand-new conversation, that you mentioned three weeks ago you're vegetarian, and adjusts a recipe suggestion accordingly — without you repeating that fact.
contentSections.question: Given lesson one's core fact (the model only operates on its current context window), what has to be true for this to work?

options.label: The model's weights were quietly retrained overnight to include this specific fact about you
A separate system stored that fact from the earlier conversation, and automatically inserted it into the context window of this new conversation, before the model ever started generating
The model has a persistent, private memory that exists independently of any context window

feedback.retrain: Retraining a model's weights in real time per user, per fact, isn't how any mainstream deployed memory feature works — it would be enormously expensive and slow, incompatible with instant recall in a new conversation.
feedback.injected: Right. This is the only option consistent with lesson one's core fact — the model itself never violates 'only the current context window' — it just so happens the current context window was pre-populated by a separate system before you typed anything.
feedback.persistent: This would directly contradict lesson one's established mechanism — there's no persistent memory store the model itself consults independent of its context window. Any 'memory' has to enter through the context window, the same door as everything else.

contentSections.mechanism: **A memory feature is an external system bolted onto the model, not a change to how the model itself works.** It stores selected facts elsewhere, and automatically inserts them into the context window of future conversations — the model is still doing exactly what module one and lesson one of this module described, just with some of its input supplied automatically instead of typed by you.

contentSections.body: A memory feature doesn't change how the model works — it changes what gets automatically placed into the context window before you start typing.

contentSections.title: Where memory features can quietly fail

contentSections.body: Once you know memory works by re-injecting stored facts into a fresh context window, two other lessons from this module immediately predict specific ways it can go wrong.

contentSections.scenario: You're evaluating whether to trust a memory feature for a specific use case: keeping track of a long-term client's project preferences over many separate conversations.
contentSections.question: Which of these are genuine risks, given how memory features actually work?

items.label: A preference that changed since it was recorded won't automatically update itself in the stored memory
If many facts are injected at once, some may be weakly attended to due to their position in the resulting context, independent of storage accuracy
The memory feature might accidentally retrain the model's weights and affect other users
A fact accurately stored from one context (a joke, a hypothetical) might get injected and treated as a straightforward true fact in a new context where that nuance is lost

explanation.staleness: A real risk, directly established — stored facts don't self-update, and nothing about the memory mechanism includes an automatic freshness check.
explanation.position: A real risk — injected memory content is ordinary context-window content once it's in, subject to the same positional effects as anything else.
explanation.retrain-risk: This doesn't follow from how memory features actually work — they don't touch model weights at all, and per-user context injection has no mechanism for leaking into other users' sessions through weight changes.
explanation.wrong-context: A real, subtler risk — a memory system storing 'facts' from a conversation can lose the surrounding nuance (sarcasm, a hypothetical, a since-reversed decision) that made the original statement not a literal, standing fact, and re-inject it flattened into something the model then treats as straightforwardly true.

contentSections.synthesis: All three real risks trace back to the same root: memory is stored and re-injected content, not genuine ongoing understanding — it inherits every limitation of context-window content (staleness, position, loss of nuance) because that's exactly what it becomes the moment it's inserted.

contentSections.body: Two concrete failure modes follow directly from mechanisms already covered. First, staleness: a stored fact doesn't expire on its own — if circumstances changed since it was recorded, the memory system has no built-in way to know that, and will keep re-inserting outdated information as though it were current, exactly the way any stored data can go stale without an update mechanism. Second, positional weakness: injected memory content becomes part of the new conversation's context window, and is just as subject to the lost-in-the-middle effect from lesson three as anything else — if a lot of memory facts get dumped in at once, some of them may be poorly attended to for exactly the same positional reasons a fact buried in a long document is, regardless of how reliably the storage and retrieval system itself worked.

Trust a memory feature the way you'd trust any re-inserted note, not the way you'd trust a person's ongoing understanding of you — it can go stale, get buried, or lose its original context, same as anything else living in a context window.

title: Starting fresh on purpose
description: A long, messy conversation doesn't just risk losing old content — everything still in it, including wrong turns and abandoned tangents, keeps shaping every new prediction. Sometimes the right move is a deliberately clean context.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate when starting a fresh conversation is preferable to continuing a long one
Construct a minimal, deliberate context to carry forward into a new conversation

contentSections.title: Old content doesn't get discounted automatically

contentSections.body: You corrected a wrong assumption fifteen messages ago. In your head, that's settled — you've moved on. In the context window, the wrong assumption and the correction are both still sitting there, in full, shaping every prediction since.

contentSections.question: Once you've corrected a model's mistake mid-conversation, does the original mistaken content get removed or discounted from the context window, or does it remain, unmarked, alongside the correction?
contentSections.answer: It remains, unmarked, alongside the correction — nothing in the mechanism automatically flags earlier content as superseded. Both the original mistake and the correction are just tokens in the same context window, both shaping every subsequent prediction, with no built-in 'ignore this part' marker.
contentSections.hint: There's no step in the generation loop from module one labeled 'discount anything the user later corrected' — the whole context window is just... the context window.

contentSections.body: This is the practical payoff of taking the mechanism seriously rather than treating a conversation like a chat with a person who naturally updates their working understanding as things get clarified. A person mentally sets aside a corrected mistake. A model's context window doesn't — the mistake, the correction, and everything said in between are all still present, all still part of what every subsequent token is conditioned on. In a short conversation this rarely matters much. In a long, winding one, with several wrong turns and course-corrections stacked up, it can genuinely degrade output quality — not because the model "forgot" the correction, but because the correction is competing with everything else in the window, including content the lost-in-the-middle effect might weight unpredictably.
A corrected mistake doesn't disappear from the context window — it just sits there next to the correction, both still shaping every prediction that follows.
If a long, messy context is itself a liability, the fix isn't trying harder within it — it's deliberately constructing a clean one.

contentSections.scenario:
You're about to start a fresh conversation to replace a long, tangent-heavy one about planning an event. Four things you could carry forward:

1. The final, agreed venue and date
2. The full back-and-forth about three venues that got rejected
3. The current, still-open question about catering
4. An earlier tangent about parking that got resolved and dropped
contentSections.question: Which of these is worth deliberately leaving out of the fresh conversation's context?

options.label: The final venue and date
The rejected-venues back-and-forth
The current open catering question
All four should be included for completeness

feedback.1: This is exactly the kind of essential, final decision worth carrying forward — it's the settled outcome, not the path to it.
feedback.2: Right. The rejected-venue discussion did its job and reached a conclusion — carrying the full back-and-forth forward just adds noise the model has to condition on, competing for attention with what's actually still relevant, for no ongoing benefit.
feedback.3: This is the live, current task — obviously worth including, since it's what the new conversation actually needs to help with.
feedback.all: This defeats the entire purpose of starting fresh — a 'clean' context that includes every abandoned tangent isn't clean at all, it's just the old conversation copy-pasted.

contentSections.concept: **A deliberately clean context carries forward final decisions and live open questions, and leaves out the path that led there.** The goal isn't completeness — it's giving the model the least noisy, most relevant input for the task actually at hand.

contentSections.body: Starting fresh isn't giving up on a conversation — it's a deliberate, structural move: construct a clean context with only what's essential, instead of asking the model to correctly discount everything that's accumulated.

title: Practice — Diagnose Eight Context-Related Failures
description: Eight drills diagnosing real conversation problems back to the specific context-window mechanism responsible. No new concepts — this is where the mechanism stops being an abstract diagram.

learningObjectives.text: Diagnose a conversational failure as a context-window mechanism rather than a knowledge or reasoning failure
Apply positional and memory-mechanism knowledge to predict and prevent context failures

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Eight drills diagnosing real failures back to cause. Take it in one sitting or spread it out — nothing expires and nothing is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Map Where One Long Conversation Degraded
description: Take a real, long conversation and annotate exactly where and why quality dropped, using this module's mechanisms rather than a vague sense that 'it got worse.'

learningObjectives.text: Identify specific points in a real long conversation where context mechanisms caused a quality drop
Produce an annotated log distinguishing context-window causes from other causes

contentSections.body: You now have three specific mechanisms — size limits, lost-in-the-middle, and memory-feature behavior — that can each degrade a long conversation in a distinct, identifiable way. This lab asks you to find a real instance of at least one of them, not a hypothetical.

contentSections.title: One conversation, annotated
contentSections.brief: Find or create a genuinely long conversation with a chat-based model — either one you already have (ideally 25+ messages, or a long document-heavy exchange) or one you deliberately build for this lab. Identify at least one real point where quality measurably dropped, and annotate exactly why, tying it to a specific mechanism from this module rather than a vague description.
contentSections.deliverable: An annotated conversation log: the point(s) where quality dropped, the specific context-window mechanism responsible, and a corrective action you'd take (re-stating a fact, repositioning an instruction, or starting fresh) with a note on whether it worked.

stages.title: Get or build a long conversation
stages.instructions: Use an existing long conversation if you have one, or deliberately build one: either a genuinely long back-and-forth (25+ messages) on an evolving task, or a single prompt with a long pasted document (10+ pages of text) plus several questions about content at different positions within it. Either approach is valid — note which one you chose and why.
stages.checkpoint: You have a real conversation or long-document exchange, saved in full, that's substantial enough to plausibly show a context effect.

stages.title: Find and mark the degradation point
stages.instructions: Read back through it looking specifically for: a detail from early on getting contradicted or lost later, a fact from deep in a pasted document being missed or mishandled, or (if using a product with memory) a stale or misapplied stored fact. Mark the exact message or location where this happens. If you don't find one on the first read, try deliberately testing for the lost-in-the-middle effect: ask about content from the middle of a long document versus the start, and compare accuracy directly.
stages.checkpoint: You have at least one specific, marked point where quality measurably dropped, with the exact evidence (what was asked, what was expected, what was actually returned).

stages.title: Diagnose the mechanism and test a fix
stages.instructions: For the point you marked, state which specific mechanism from this module is responsible — size limit, lost-in-the-middle, or memory staleness — and why, ruling out the other two. Then try one corrective action (re-state the fact explicitly, move a critical instruction to the start or end, or start a fresh conversation with a minimal clean context) and record whether it actually fixed the issue.
stages.checkpoint: You have a specific mechanism attribution with reasoning, one corrective action actually attempted, and an honest record of whether it worked.

stages.title: Write it up
stages.instructions: Assemble the annotated log: the original evidence, your mechanism diagnosis, the fix you tried, and the result. Close with one sentence on what you'd do differently from the start of a similar conversation, given what you now know.
stages.checkpoint: The write-up is complete and could be understood by someone who didn't see the original conversation.

rubric.criterion: The degradation point is real, not hypothetical
rubric.meets: The log includes actual message text or document excerpts showing exactly where and how quality dropped, not a general description.

rubric.criterion: The mechanism attribution is specific and justified
rubric.meets: One of the three mechanisms (size limit, position, memory) is named, with reasoning for why it fits better than the other two.

rubric.criterion: A real corrective action was attempted
rubric.meets: The write-up shows an actual fix being tried in the conversation, not just a proposed fix left untested.

rubric.criterion: The result of the fix is reported honestly
rubric.meets: Whether the fix worked, partially worked, or didn't work is stated plainly, without exaggerating success.

rubric.criterion: The closing lesson is specific
rubric.meets: The final sentence names a concrete practice to adopt, not a general statement like 'be more careful with long conversations.'

rubric.criterion: The log is usable by someone who wasn't there
rubric.meets: A reader unfamiliar with the original conversation could follow the evidence, diagnosis, and fix without needing more context.

contentSections.body: Finding a real degradation point and correctly attributing it to a specific mechanism is what turns 'long conversations get worse sometimes' from a vague complaint into something you can actually work around.

title: Checkpoint — The Context Window
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four reaching back to training, two reaching further back to prediction. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's context mechanisms alongside earlier modules' material

questions.from: This module — The Context Window
questions.prompt: When you start a brand-new conversation with no memory feature enabled, how much does the model know about a previous, separate conversation?

options.label: Nothing — it starts with an empty context window
A vague, faded sense of it, like a person's memory
Everything, since it was trained on many conversations

questions.explanation: The model only ever operates on the current context window — a new conversation is genuinely empty of any prior conversation's content by default.

questions.from: This module — The Context Window
questions.prompt: What happens when a conversation's token count exceeds the context window's size limit?

options.label: The window silently expands to fit
Something has to give — commonly the oldest content is dropped, truncated, or summarized, even if the visible chat history still shows it
The conversation stops functioning entirely

questions.explanation: A context window is a fixed-size input; excess content has to be handled somehow, and the visible interface history isn't proof of what the model actually still has access to.

questions.from: This module — The Context Window
questions.prompt: What does the 'lost in the middle' effect describe?

options.label: Content buried in the middle of a long context tends to be retrieved less reliably than content near the start or end, even when everything technically fits
Middle-length documents are processed faster than short or long ones
The middle of a conversation is always the most accurate part

questions.explanation: Position within a context window is a separate factor from total size — the middle is a documented weak spot for retrieval reliability.

questions.from: This module — The Context Window
questions.prompt: Mechanistically, how does a chat product's 'memory' feature actually work?

options.label: It retrains the model's weights in real time per user
A separate system stores facts and automatically re-inserts them into the context window of new conversations — the model still only ever sees its current context window
It has no real mechanism, it's purely marketing

questions.explanation: Memory is an external system bolted around the model, not a change to how the model itself operates.

questions.from: This module — The Context Window
questions.prompt: Once a mistake is corrected mid-conversation, what happens to the original mistaken content in the context window?

options.label: It's automatically removed once corrected
It remains, unmarked, alongside the correction, still shaping every subsequent prediction
It gets replaced by the correction in place

questions.explanation: Nothing flags superseded content as ignorable — both the mistake and the correction persist in the context window equally.

questions.from: Previous module — Where the Behaviour Comes From
questions.prompt: Why doesn't pre-training automatically distinguish reliable text sources from unreliable ones?

options.label: The next-token-prediction objective has no built-in reliability check — filtering has to be a deliberate, separate curatorial decision
It does, using a built-in fact-checking pass
Only reliable sources are ever included in training corpora

questions.explanation: Whatever isn't filtered out beforehand shapes the model's statistics in proportion to volume, not trustworthiness.

questions.from: Previous module — Where the Behaviour Comes From
questions.prompt: What does RLHF actually optimize for?

options.label: A directly measured, automated accuracy score
