Aggregate human rater preference between compared responses, which correlates with but isn't identical to accuracy
The shortest possible correct answer

questions.explanation: The reward model is trained on human preference comparisons, not a ground-truth check.

questions.from: Previous module — Where the Behaviour Comes From
questions.prompt: Why can't a single later training pass fully remove bias from a model?

options.label: Bias can enter independently at multiple stages — corpus composition, fine-tuning example selection, and the rater pool — and a later pass doesn't reach the earlier ones
Bias is impossible to address at any stage
A single pass can actually remove it completely

questions.explanation: Each training stage is an independent opportunity for skew to enter.

questions.from: Three modules back — Prediction, Not Thinking
questions.prompt: In one sentence, what does a language model do to produce each token of its output?

options.label: Computes a probability distribution over the next token given everything so far, and samples one
Looks up the most relevant fact in a stored knowledge base
Plans the full response before writing any of it

questions.explanation: The complete mechanism from module one, still exactly what's running underneath everything covered since.

questions.from: Three modules back — Prediction, Not Thinking
questions.prompt: What combination of factors carries the highest fabrication risk?

options.label: A well-known general fact stated approximately
An obscure topic combined with a request for an exact, precise detail
Any question phrased as a complete sentence

questions.explanation: Obscurity means thin training signal; precision removes any safe middle ground — together they're close to a worst case.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: Temperature and randomness, demonstrated
description: Temperature governs how a token gets picked from the probability distribution computed in module one — and choosing it deliberately is the first lever this module covers.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what temperature controls in the token-selection process
Choose an appropriate temperature setting for a given task

contentSections.title: The step after the probability distribution

contentSections.body: Send "write one sentence about autumn" to a model three separate times, same settings, and you can get three genuinely different sentences. Module one said every token comes from a probability distribution — this is the setting that decides what happens to that distribution next.

contentSections.question: If a token has a 30% probability of being next, according to the model's computed distribution, and you're sampling at a moderate non-zero temperature, roughly how often will that token actually get selected across many repeated generations?
contentSections.answer: Roughly 30% of the time — sampling at non-zero temperature genuinely respects the probabilities, rather than always picking the single most likely token. A lower-probability token can and does get selected sometimes, proportional to its own probability.
contentSections.hint: "Sampling" means the probabilities are treated as real odds, not just a ranking.

contentSections.body: Temperature is applied to the probability distribution before a token is picked from it. A low temperature sharpens the distribution — it pushes more of the probability mass toward the already-most-likely tokens, making the choice closer to always picking the single top candidate (at temperature zero, that's exactly what happens: the same highest-probability token every time, deterministically). A higher temperature flattens the distribution — it gives lower-probability tokens a more meaningful chance of being picked, producing more varied, sometimes more surprising output, at the cost of also raising the chance of picking something genuinely worse.

contentSections.question: Put these steps of generating one token, with a non-zero temperature, in the order they actually happen.
steps: The model computes a raw probability distribution over the vocabulary for the next token
Temperature is applied to that distribution, sharpening or flattening it
A token is sampled from the adjusted distribution, weighted by the resulting probabilities
The sampled token is appended to the sequence
contentSections.explanation: Temperature modifies the distribution itself before sampling happens — it doesn't change which tokens are possible, only how sharply the probabilities favor the top candidates versus spreading chances across more of them.

contentSections.body: Temperature doesn't change what the model 'thinks' is likely — it changes how strictly that likelihood is respected when actually picking a token.
A brainstorming tool and an invoice-parsing tool built on the same underlying model can — and should — use completely different temperature settings, for opposite reasons.

contentSections.scenario:
Four real tasks a product might use a model for:

1. Generating five varied slogan options for a new product
2. Extracting a customer's account number from a support ticket
3. Writing a short creative poem on request
4. Converting a spoken date ("the fifteenth of next month") into a fixed calendar format
contentSections.question: Which two of these clearly call for a LOW temperature (favoring the single most likely, most reliable output)?

options.label: 1 and 3 — the two creative tasks
2 and 4 — the two tasks with one correct answer
All four benefit equally from a high temperature

feedback.creative: These are exactly backwards for temperature purposes — the creative tasks are where variety is the point, so a *higher* temperature serves them, not a lower one.
feedback.precise: Right. Extracting an account number and converting a date both have a single correct output — any randomness introduced by a higher temperature is pure downside here, with no benefit to offset it.
feedback.all-high: A high temperature actively hurts the two precision tasks — there's no upside to variety when there's exactly one right answer, and real downside if the sampled token happens to be a lower-probability, wrong one.

contentSections.concept: **Temperature should track whether a task has one correct answer or benefits from variety — not be left at a single default for everything.** Precision tasks want it low; generative, creative, brainstorming tasks want it higher.

contentSections.body: This is a genuinely practical lever, not a cosmetic one. Many products ship with a single default temperature tuned for general conversational use, which is a reasonable middle ground but not optimal for every task run through the same model. Anywhere a task has a single correct or clearly-best answer — data extraction, classification, format conversion, factual lookup — pushing temperature down reduces unnecessary variance. Anywhere the task explicitly benefits from a range of options — brainstorming, creative writing, generating varied examples — pushing it up is what makes the feature actually useful rather than repetitive.
Choose temperature by asking whether the task has one right answer (go low) or benefits from variety (go higher) — not by leaving it at whatever the default happens to be.

title: Why the same prompt gives different answers
description: Sampling is the main source of run-to-run variation, and temperature zero mostly but not perfectly eliminates it — worth knowing precisely, especially if you're testing or automating around a model's output.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why identical prompts can produce different outputs, and when they mostly won't
Design a testing approach that accounts for output variability

contentSections.body: "Just set temperature to zero and it'll be deterministic" is close to true, and the gap between close and exactly true is worth knowing about before you build something that depends on it.

contentSections.scenario: A developer sets temperature to exactly zero for a production feature and, in rare cases (maybe one in several thousand identical requests), still sees a slightly different output.
contentSections.question: Given that temperature zero removes probabilistic sampling, what's the most plausible remaining source of this rare variation?

options.label: Temperature zero doesn't actually do anything

Tiny floating-point computation differences, which can occur under certain parallel/batched inference conditions on real hardware, occasionally flip which token scores as marginally highest in an extremely close tie
The model is deliberately reintroducing randomness to seem more 'natural'

feedback.no-effect: Temperature zero has a very real, large effect — it removes the deliberate probabilistic sampling step almost entirely, which is why output is close to identical, not because it does nothing.
feedback.floating-point: Right. Real inference systems run on hardware doing lots of parallel computation, often batched together with other requests — computation order can vary slightly, and in rare very-close-probability ties, that can flip which token comes out marginally ahead. This is a separate, secondary source of variation from the sampling behavior temperature directly controls.
feedback.deliberate: There's no mechanism or incentive for a system to secretly reintroduce randomness after you've explicitly asked for temperature zero — this isn't a deliberate behavior.

contentSections.mechanism: **Temperature zero removes deliberate probabilistic sampling, which is the main and largest source of output variation — it does not guarantee perfect bit-for-bit determinism against every possible source of variation in a real running system.** Close to deterministic, with a rare and separate source of tiny variation, is the accurate claim.

contentSections.body: Temperature zero removes the main source of run-to-run variation — treat it as close-to-deterministic in practice, not as an absolute mathematical guarantee.

contentSections.title: Building around variability instead of fighting it

contentSections.body: A QA engineer's automated test keeps failing on a feature that's working fine — because the test expects exact string equality, and the model's output at a normal (non-zero) temperature genuinely, legitimately varies run to run.

contentSections.scenario: You're designing an automated testing strategy for a feature built on a model with a moderate, non-zero temperature in production.
contentSections.question: Which of these are genuinely useful approaches, given everything in this lesson?

items.label: Use temperature zero specifically in the test environment, even if production uses a higher value, to get reproducible test runs
Test structural or semantic properties of the output (valid format, required fields present, passes a rubric) instead of exact string matching
Assert the output exactly matches one fixed reference string, for a feature using a non-zero production temperature
Run the same test input multiple times and check that outputs stay within an expected range or pattern, rather than expecting one single value

explanation.test-temp-zero: Useful and common — trading exact production fidelity for a reproducible test signal is often a reasonable choice, as long as you're honest that it's testing a slightly different configuration.
explanation.property-checks: Genuinely the most robust approach for most cases — it tests what actually matters (is the output usable and correct in structure) rather than an accident of exact phrasing.
explanation.exact-match: This is the brittle approach that predictably breaks against a feature using non-zero temperature by design — the test will report false failures for legitimately varied, equally-valid outputs.
explanation.multiple-runs: A genuinely useful technique — sampling several runs and checking the *distribution* of outputs matches expectations is often more informative than checking any single run in isolation.

contentSections.synthesis: The common thread across the useful approaches: they work *with* the fact that generation is probabilistic by design, rather than pretending it's deterministic when the production configuration says otherwise.

contentSections.body: This isn't purely a testing-team concern — it generalizes to anywhere someone builds an automated pipeline around model output and implicitly assumes stability that a non-zero temperature doesn't actually provide. The fix is never "complain that the model is inconsistent" — it's matching your tolerance for variation to the setting that's actually controlling it.

Build tests and pipelines around what temperature actually promises — near-determinism at zero, genuine variation above it — instead of assuming stability a non-zero setting was never going to provide.

title: System instructions versus what you type
description: System instructions and user messages are both just tokens in the same context window — what makes system instructions different is training, not a separate enforcement mechanism, and that has real consequences for how reliable they are.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why system instructions carry more weight than user messages, mechanistically
Apply this understanding to predict when system instructions can be overridden by sustained user pressure

contentSections.title: Two kinds of instruction, one mechanism

contentSections.body: A support chatbot is unfailingly polite, on-brand, and concise — before the user has typed anything. That behavior came from somewhere the user never sees: a system instruction, sitting in the context window before the conversation even starts.

contentSections.question: Mechanically, is a hidden system instruction processed by a fundamentally different part of the model than a user's typed message, or is it the same mechanism treating the same kind of input differently because of how it was trained?
contentSections.answer: The same mechanism — a system instruction is still just tokens in the same context window, processed by the identical next-token-prediction mechanism from module one. What's different is that training specifically teaches the model to weight system-role content as higher-priority framing, not a separate enforcement system running alongside it.
contentSections.hint: There's no second engine bolted onto the model specifically for system instructions — everything still goes through the one mechanism from module one.

contentSections.body: This distinction matters because it explains both why system instructions are genuinely effective and why they aren't absolute. A product's system instruction ("you are a support agent, stay on brand, keep answers short") sits at the start of the context window, and the model has been specifically trained — through instruction fine-tuning and RLHF, both covered in the previous module — to treat that framing as governing everything that follows, more heavily than it weights an ordinary user request. That's a real, trained behavior, not a fiction. But it's still fundamentally the same prediction mechanism, working from the same context window, which means it's a strong statistical tendency rather than a hard, unbreakable rule enforced by something outside the model.

contentSections.code: Product documentation claim: "Our system instructions are enforced at the model level and cannot be overridden by anything a user types, guaranteed."
contentSections.question: What's the overreach in this claim, given the mechanism covered so far?

options.label: System instructions are a strongly-trained tendency operating through the same prediction mechanism as user messages — not a separate, hardcoded enforcement layer that guarantees an unbreakable rule
The claim is entirely accurate — system instructions really are a separate, unbreakable enforcement layer
System instructions have no real effect at all, so the claim is meaningless either way

contentSections.flawExplanation: "Guaranteed" and "cannot be overridden" describe a hard enforcement mechanism that doesn't exist at the model level — everything, system instruction and user message alike, goes through the same next-token-prediction mechanism, just with system-role content trained to carry more weight. That's a strong, usually reliable tendency, genuinely useful for shaping default behavior — but claiming it as an absolute guarantee overstates what training-shaped behavior can promise, which is exactly why real production systems needing hard guarantees layer separate, non-model safeguards on top rather than relying on the instruction alone.

contentSections.body: A system instruction is a strongly-trained priority, not a separate enforcement mechanism — it works through the exact same context-window-based prediction as everything else, which is both why it usually works and why it isn't unbreakable.

A user, insistent and persistent across many messages, sometimes manages to get a chatbot to partially drift from its system instruction. Does that mean the instruction failed, or is this exactly what the mechanism predicts?

contentSections.intro: You're designing a system instruction for an internal tool that summarizes legal documents, and you specifically need it to always include a disclaimer that it's not legal advice — a requirement that genuinely matters and shouldn't be easy to accidentally drop through normal conversation drift.

fields.question: Where should the disclaimer requirement sit for maximum reliability, given what you know about context-window position from the previous module and system-instruction weighting from this one?

options.label: Only once, buried in the middle of a long system instruction
Clearly stated in the system instruction, and reinforced by a separate, non-model check on the final output before it's shown to the user
Left to the user to remember to ask for each time

feedback.buried: This combines two real weaknesses: burying a critical instruction risks the lost-in-the-middle effect, and relying on the system instruction alone for something that genuinely must not fail risks the instruction-weighting-can-bend issue from this lesson.
feedback.layered: This is the robust choice — the system instruction does the normal, usually-reliable job of shaping default behavior, and a separate, non-model check (verifying the disclaimer text is actually present before output is shown) provides the hard guarantee that a trained tendency alone can't promise.
feedback.user-burden: This defeats the purpose of a system instruction entirely, and puts a requirement that matters for compliance in the least reliable place — depending on every user remembering to ask.

contentSections.synthesis: For anything that has to be genuinely reliable — not just usually-true — the pattern is: use the system instruction for what it's good at (shaping default behavior efficiently) and add a separate, non-model safeguard for what it can't guarantee (an absolute, unbreakable requirement).

contentSections.body: This is the practical takeaway worth carrying forward: system instructions are a genuinely useful, efficient lever — far better than expecting every user to restate the same constraints every time — but they inherit the same statistical, not absolute, nature as everything else this track has covered. For anything low-stakes (tone, default format, general persona), that reliability is more than sufficient. For anything that must never fail (a legal disclaimer, a safety constraint, a compliance requirement), pair the system instruction with an independent check outside the model, rather than trusting the instruction alone to hold under any amount of pressure.
Use system instructions for what strongly-trained-but-not-absolute weighting is good at, and back up anything that genuinely can't fail with a separate, non-model check.

title: Length limits and answers that stop mid-thought
description: A response cut off mid-sentence isn't the model changing its mind — it's an external length cap that doesn't care where the model was in the middle of saying something.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a natural model stopping point from an externally-imposed length cap
Design a strategy for handling generation that risks hitting a length limit

contentSections.body: A model's answer ends mid-sentence, an unclosed bracket hanging in the code. It didn't decide to stop there — it ran out of room.

contentSections.scenario: Two different responses from the same model. Response A ends cleanly, with a complete final sentence and no dangling structure. Response B ends abruptly, mid-word, with an unclosed parenthesis.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely difference between how these two generations actually stopped?

options.label: Response A hit its natural learned stopping point; response B was cut off by an external maximum length limit before it reached one
Both stopped for the exact same reason, and B just happened to be a worse answer
Response B stopped because the topic was too difficult

feedback.two-mechanisms: Right. A model learns to produce its own end-of-response signal when it judges a reply complete — that's what produces clean endings like response A. An external token cap has no awareness of sentence or structural boundaries at all — hitting it mid-generation produces exactly the abrupt, structurally broken cutoff response B shows.
feedback.same-reason: The mechanism is genuinely different, not just a difference in quality — a clean ending and a mid-bracket cutoff come from two distinct stopping conditions, one internal to the model's learned behavior and one external and indifferent to content.
feedback.difficulty: Topic difficulty might affect content quality, but it doesn't explain a mid-word, structurally broken cutoff specifically — that's the signature of an external limit, not of the model struggling with the content.

contentSections.mechanism: **Generation stops for one of two reasons: the model reaches its own learned end-of-response point, or an external maximum length is hit first.** Only the first one produces clean, complete endings — the second doesn't know or care what it's cutting off.

contentSections.body: A response cut off mid-structure is an external length cap, not the model choosing to stop there — the two have completely different signatures and completely different fixes.
"Just raise the length limit" works until it doesn't — longer limits cost more and take longer, and some tasks will always eventually be long enough to risk hitting even a generous cap.

contentSections.scenario: You're building a feature that occasionally generates long, structured content and sometimes hits the configured length limit partway through.
contentSections.question: Which of these are genuinely useful strategies, beyond simply raising the limit further?

items.label: Break the task into smaller sections, each requested as its own generation with its own, comfortably-sufficient length budget
Programmatically detect a truncated response and issue a continuation request to pick up where it left off
Ignore the issue, since it only happens occasionally on the longest outputs
On truncation, simply retry the exact same full request from scratch and hope it fits this time

explanation.chunking: A genuinely robust strategy — smaller, well-scoped generations are much less likely to individually approach the length cap, and it composes well with the context-window lessons on giving the model a focused, less crowded task.
explanation.detect-continue: A genuinely useful strategy for handling the cases that do occur — detecting the specific signature of truncation (no natural stop marker, hit exactly the token cap, structurally incomplete) and requesting a targeted continuation is far more efficient than starting over.
explanation.ignore: Not a real strategy — 'occasionally' at scale, across many users and requests, adds up to a real, recurring failure mode worth designing around rather than accepting as unavoidable noise.
explanation.retry-same: Retrying the identical full-length request doesn't address the underlying cause — if the content genuinely needs more room than the limit allows, an identical retry is likely to hit the same wall again, wasting a full generation for no gain.

contentSections.synthesis: The two real strategies share a principle: work with the length limit as a known, fixed constraint — chunk what can be broken into pieces, and handle what can't be chunked with targeted detection and continuation, rather than treating the constraint as something to just hope you don't hit.

contentSections.body: The underlying discipline here connects back to the previous lesson's system-instruction material: length limits, like everything else covered in this module, are a real, fixed engineering constraint, not a quality problem with the model to be worked around by hoping harder. Designing for it — chunking naturally-long tasks, detecting and handling truncation explicitly — produces a feature that behaves predictably at the edges, instead of one that occasionally, silently hands a user a broken half-answer.
Design for the length limit as a known constraint — chunk what can be chunked, detect and continue what can't — rather than treating an occasional truncated response as an unavoidable surprise.

title: Reasoning modes and what they cost you
description: Reasoning modes don't add a new mechanism — they spend more tokens on the same next-token prediction, generating intermediate steps before the final answer, and that spending has real costs worth weighing deliberately.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what a reasoning mode actually does mechanistically
Evaluate when the latency and cost of reasoning mode are worth paying

contentSections.body: Turn on a "reasoning" or "extended thinking" option and watch a model visibly work through a multi-step problem before answering — and get it right noticeably more often than it did jumping straight to an answer. Does this mean something fundamentally different is happening under the hood?

contentSections.scenario: A reasoning-mode response to a genuinely hard multi-step problem generates a visible or hidden scratchpad of intermediate steps before the final answer, in addition to the answer itself.
contentSections.question: Roughly how many times more tokens might a reasoning-mode response generate, compared to the same model asked to answer directly with no reasoning steps, for a genuinely hard problem?
contentSections.explanation: This varies enormously by problem and by how extensively reasoning mode is configured to work, but it's common for a hard problem's reasoning trace to run several times longer than a direct answer would — sometimes far more. The exact multiplier matters less than the takeaway: this is real, additional token generation, not a free upgrade, and every one of those tokens costs money and time exactly the way any other generated token does.

contentSections.body: Nothing about reasoning mode introduces a new kind of computation separate from next-token prediction — it's the same mechanism from module one, used differently. Instead of jumping straight from the prompt to a final answer in one continuous prediction, the model generates a longer sequence of intermediate tokens first — working through the problem in text, step by step, each step conditioned on the steps before it, the same autoregressive process as always. That extra room to work through a problem incrementally, rather than committing to an answer in one jump, is genuinely what improves accuracy on multi-step problems — but it's still prediction all the way down, just with more predicted tokens standing between the prompt and the final answer.
Reasoning mode doesn't add a new capability separate from token prediction — it spends more predicted tokens working through a problem step by step before committing to an answer.

contentSections.title: What that extra spending actually costs

contentSections.body: If reasoning mode is just more tokens, it has the same bill as more tokens anywhere else in this track: real money, and real time waiting for a response. Whether that's worth paying depends entirely on the task.

contentSections.scenario:
Four requests a product might route through a model with a reasoning mode option:

1. "What's 847 divided by 23, and is the result a whole number?"
2. "What's today's date in ISO 8601 format?"
3. "Plan a multi-step approach to reduce a database's query latency, considering three possible bottlenecks and their tradeoffs"
4. "Capitalize this sentence correctly."
contentSections.question: Which two of these are the strongest candidates for enabling reasoning mode?

options.label: 1 and 3 — the ones with genuine multi-step reasoning or calculation
2 and 4 — the simple formatting and lookup tasks
All four benefit equally from reasoning mode

feedback.reasoning-tasks: Right. The division-and-verification problem and the multi-bottleneck planning problem both plausibly benefit from working through intermediate steps rather than jumping straight to an answer — exactly where the previous pod's mechanism predicts a real accuracy gain worth the extra cost.
feedback.simple-tasks: These are exactly backwards — a date format lookup and a capitalization fix don't need multi-step reasoning to get right, so enabling reasoning mode here pays the latency and token cost with essentially no accuracy benefit to show for it.
feedback.all-equal: Reasoning mode's benefit is specifically tied to whether a task requires working through multiple steps — a simple, single-jump lookup or formatting task gains nothing from extra reasoning tokens it didn't need.

contentSections.concept: **Reasoning mode is worth its cost specifically where a task benefits from multiple, incremental steps rather than a single confident jump to an answer.** Applying it universally pays the latency and token cost on every request, including the large share that were never going to benefit from it.

contentSections.body: This is the same discipline as temperature from the first lesson of this module, applied to a different setting: match the tool to the task, deliberately, rather than picking one default and leaving it there for everything. Reasoning mode is a genuine, real capability improvement for the right tasks — and a straightforward waste of latency and money for the ones that never needed it. Knowing which is which, given the mechanism, is the actual skill; "turn it on for everything to be safe" isn't free, and "never use it" throws away a real accuracy gain on the problems that need it.
Reasoning mode is worth its real latency and token cost specifically for genuinely multi-step problems — enabling it universally spends that cost on tasks that were never going to benefit.

title: Practice — Choose Settings for Eight Tasks
description: Eight drills matching the right setting to the right task. No new concepts — this is where knowing what temperature does turns into knowing when to change it.

learningObjectives.text: Select an appropriate temperature, instruction placement, or reasoning-mode setting for a given task
Diagnose which setting produced an observed model behavior

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Eight drills matching settings to tasks and diagnosing behavior back to cause. Take it in one sitting or spread it out — nothing expires and nothing is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Run the Same Task Across Settings and Compare
description: Pick one real task, run it across genuinely different settings, and build the comparison this whole module has been arguing for — with actual evidence instead of a general impression.

learningObjectives.text: Systematically vary one setting across a fixed task and observe the effect
Draw a defensible, evidence-based conclusion about which settings suit which task

contentSections.body: This module has argued, lesson after lesson, that settings should match the task rather than sit at a default. This lab asks you to actually build the evidence for that, on one real task you choose, instead of taking the module's word for it.

contentSections.title: One task, several settings, compared honestly
contentSections.brief: Pick one real task you'd actually want a model's help with. Run it across at least three genuinely different settings configurations (varying temperature, and/or a system instruction, and/or a reasoning mode if available to you), and build a comparison table with your own stated recommendation for which setting actually fits this task best, and why.
contentSections.deliverable: A comparison table of the same task run under at least three different settings configurations, with the actual outputs, a brief evaluation of each, and a stated recommendation with reasoning tied to this module's mechanisms.

stages.title: Pick a real task and define what 'better' means for it
stages.instructions: Choose a real task — something you'd genuinely use a model for, not a toy example. Before running anything, write down what would make one output better than another for this specific task: is it correctness, variety, conciseness, creativity, something else? This matters because 'better' means different things for different tasks, exactly as this module argued.
stages.checkpoint: You have a specific task and a written, specific definition of what a better output looks like for it.

stages.title: Run it across at least three settings configurations
stages.instructions: Run the identical task prompt across at least three meaningfully different settings — for example: low temperature vs. high temperature; with vs. without a system instruction; with vs. without reasoning mode enabled, if available to you. Save every output in full. If you can only vary temperature (some tools don't expose system instructions or reasoning mode), that's fine — vary it across at least three distinct values.
stages.checkpoint: You have at least three full outputs, each clearly labeled with the exact settings used to produce it.

stages.title: Build the comparison and recommend
stages.instructions: Build a table comparing the outputs against the 'better' definition you wrote in stage one. Then write a specific recommendation: which setting actually suits this task, and why, referencing the specific mechanism from this module (not just 'this one seemed nicer'). If the results surprised you — a setting you expected to help didn't, or vice versa — say so honestly and try to explain why using the mechanism.
stages.checkpoint: You have a completed comparison table and a specific, mechanism-based recommendation, including an honest note on anything that surprised you.

rubric.criterion: The task is real and specific
rubric.meets: The chosen task is something genuinely useful, not a generic placeholder, and the 'better' definition was written before seeing results.

rubric.criterion: At least three genuinely different settings configurations were tested
rubric.meets: The comparison includes at least three distinct, clearly-labeled settings configurations, not minor variations on the same setting.

rubric.criterion: All outputs are included in full
rubric.meets: Each configuration's actual output is present, not summarized or described secondhand.

rubric.criterion: The recommendation is mechanism-based, not just a preference
rubric.meets: The stated recommendation explicitly references why a setting suits the task, using this module's mechanisms (sampling behavior, instruction weighting, token budget), not just 'this one felt better.'

rubric.criterion: Surprising results are reported honestly
rubric.meets: If any result contradicted expectations, it's noted plainly along with an attempted mechanism-based explanation, rather than smoothed over.

rubric.criterion: The comparison is usable by someone else
rubric.meets: A reader unfamiliar with the task could understand what was tested, what happened, and why the recommendation follows from it.

contentSections.body: Building one real, evidence-based comparison — instead of a general impression that 'settings matter' — is what turns this module's arguments into something you can actually apply with confidence next time.

title: Checkpoint — The Settings That Change the Output
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four reaching back to the context window, two reaching further back to training. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's settings mechanisms alongside earlier modules' material

contentSections.title: Checkpoint — The Settings That Change the Output

questions.from: This module — The Settings That Change the Output
questions.prompt: What does temperature actually control?

options.label: How the probability distribution over the next token gets sampled from — low temperature favors the top candidate almost exclusively, high temperature gives lower-probability tokens a more meaningful chance
How many tokens the model is allowed to generate in total
Whether the model follows a system instruction

questions.explanation: Temperature is applied to the probability distribution before a token is sampled from it — it's a sampling-behavior setting, not a length or instruction-following setting.

questions.from: This module — The Settings That Change the Output
questions.prompt: Does temperature zero guarantee perfectly identical output on every run, with zero exceptions?

options.label: Yes, always, on any system
It removes the main source of variation (sampling) and is close to deterministic in practice, but rare floating-point differences on real hardware can still occasionally introduce tiny variation
No, temperature has no effect on consistency at all

questions.explanation: Close to deterministic is the accurate claim — not an absolute mathematical guarantee against every possible source of variation in a real running system.

questions.from: This module — The Settings That Change the Output
questions.prompt: Mechanistically, what makes a system instruction different from a user message?

options.label: It's processed by a completely separate, hardcoded enforcement system
Both are just tokens in the same context window, processed by the same prediction mechanism — training specifically teaches the model to weight system-role content as higher-priority framing
System instructions are literally invisible to the underlying model

questions.explanation: There's no separate enforcement layer — it's the same mechanism, with training-shaped weighting, which is why it's usually reliable but not absolute.

questions.from: This module — The Settings That Change the Output
questions.prompt: Why does a response sometimes cut off mid-sentence with an unclosed bracket?

options.label: The model decided that was a good stopping point
An external maximum output length limit was hit before the model reached its own natural, learned stopping point
The topic was too difficult for the model

questions.explanation: A clean ending and a mid-structure cutoff are two different mechanisms — the second is the signature of an external length cap, indifferent to content.

questions.from: Previous module — The Context Window
questions.prompt: What does the 'lost in the middle' effect describe?

options.label: Content buried in the middle of a long context tends to be retrieved less reliably than content near the start or end
Middle-length documents process faster than short or long ones
The middle of a conversation is always the most accurate part

questions.explanation: Position within a context window is a separate factor from total size.

questions.from: Previous module — The Context Window
questions.prompt: Mechanistically, how does a chat product's 'memory' feature actually work?

options.label: It retrains the model's weights in real time per user
A separate system stores facts and automatically re-inserts them into the context window of new conversations
It has no real mechanism at all

questions.explanation: Memory is an external system bolted around the model, not a change to how the model itself operates.

questions.from: Previous module — The Context Window
questions.prompt: When you start a brand-new conversation with no memory feature, how much does the model know about a previous, separate conversation?

options.label: Nothing — it starts with an empty context window
A faded, partial memory of it
Everything, since it was trained on many conversations

questions.explanation: The model only ever operates on the current context window.

questions.from: Previous module — The Context Window
questions.prompt: What happens when a conversation's token count exceeds the context window's size limit?

options.label: The window silently expands to fit
Something has to give — the oldest content is commonly dropped, truncated, or summarized
The conversation stops functioning entirely

questions.explanation: A context window is a fixed-size input; the visible chat history isn't proof of what the model actually still has access to.

questions.from: Two modules back — Where the Behaviour Comes From
questions.prompt: Why can RLHF produce sycophancy without anyone training for it directly?

options.label: Raters, comparing responses without independently fact-checking every claim, tend to find agreement more pleasant than correction on average, and that preference shapes the reward signal
Sycophancy is explicitly written into the reward model's objective
It only happens with poorly-trained reward models

questions.explanation: It's a predictable byproduct of optimizing for aggregate preference rather than a direct measure of truth.

questions.from: Two modules back — Where the Behaviour Comes From
questions.prompt: Why doesn't a raw, pre-trained-only model reliably answer a direct question instead of continuing it as a pattern?

options.label: It hasn't been taught the specific 'answer directly and stop' behavior — that's what instruction fine-tuning adds
It doesn't understand the question
It refuses instructions on principle

questions.explanation: Instruction fine-tuning is the specific stage that shifts the dominant pattern toward answering directly rather than continuing a worksheet-like shape.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: What actually differs between models
description: Every model in scope shares the same mechanism from module one — what actually varies is the specific choices made at each training stage from module two, and that's what this whole module is about learning to evaluate.

learningObjectives.text: Explain that models share a mechanism but differ through training-stage choices
Evaluate the claim that model choice 'doesn't matter' since the underlying technology is shared

contentSections.body: Two models, two different companies, the same basic description: "a large language model." Ask them the same question and you can get meaningfully different answers, different tones, different strengths. If the mechanism is the same, where does the difference actually come from?

contentSections.question: If two models share the exact same underlying mechanism (next-token prediction, shaped by pre-training, fine-tuning, and RLHF), what's the most likely source of real behavioral differences between them?
contentSections.answer: The specific choices made at each training stage — what data went into pre-training, how large the model is, which fine-tuning examples were selected, and which human raters shaped the RLHF stage. Same recipe, different ingredients and choices, different result.
contentSections.hint: Module two spent an entire module establishing that training-stage choices, not the mechanism itself, are where a model's specific behavior comes from — that logic applies just as much to comparing two different models as it did to explaining one model's quirks.

contentSections.body: Model comparison sites and marketing pages tend to talk about differences in terms of headline numbers — parameter counts, benchmark scores, release dates — which can obscure the more useful underlying fact: every one of these differences traces back to real choices made during the training pipeline from module two. A model trained heavily on code behaves differently on coding tasks than one trained on a more general mix. A model whose RLHF rater pool skewed toward one kind of task (say, long, thorough answers) will show that skew in its behavior on unrelated tasks too. None of this requires a different mechanism — it's the same mechanism, run on different inputs at every stage.

contentSections.scenario: Two models are compared. Model A was pre-trained with a heavy emphasis on code and technical documentation. Model B was pre-trained with a broader mix skewed toward general web text, news, and conversational content. Both went through similar fine-tuning and RLHF processes.
contentSections.question: Which is the more accurate prediction, given what module two established about training-stage effects?

options.label: Model A will likely be noticeably stronger on coding-related tasks; Model B may be more comfortable with general conversational tasks
They'll perform identically on everything, since the mechanism is the same
Model A will be strictly better at everything, since code is a more 'rigorous' training signal

feedback.predictable-diff: Right — this is a direct, predictable consequence of the corpus-composition mechanism from module two, applied to comparing two different models instead of explaining one model's behavior.
feedback.identical: This ignores everything module two established about how corpus composition shapes learned statistics — different training emphasis reliably produces different strengths, not identical behavior.
feedback.strictly-better: There's no reason emphasis on one domain in training makes a model 'strictly better' across the board — it predicts a specific strength in that domain, not general superiority, and likely comes with relatively weaker signal somewhere the corpus emphasized less.

contentSections.concept: **Training-stage differences predict specific, domain-shaped strengths and weaknesses between models — not one model being uniformly 'better,' and not models being identical because they share a mechanism.**

contentSections.body: Two models sharing the exact same mechanism can still differ meaningfully — the difference lives in the training-stage choices, not in the mechanism itself.

contentSections.title: Why this actually matters for choosing

contentSections.body: "They're all basically the same technology, so it doesn't matter which one you use" sounds reasonable and is subtly wrong — in a way this whole module is built to fix.

contentSections.scenario: You're deciding how to evaluate whether "model choice matters" for a specific real use case.
contentSections.question: Which of these are legitimate, evidence-based reasons two models might genuinely differ for a given task?

items.label: Different emphasis in what each model's pre-training corpus contained
Different fine-tuning examples curated toward different intended use cases
Different RLHF rater pools with different implicit preferences
Which company's name is more widely recognized

explanation.corpus-emphasis: A legitimate, mechanism-grounded reason — this is exactly what module two's pre-training material predicts will produce real behavioral differences.
explanation.finetune-target: A legitimate reason — a model fine-tuned specifically for, say, customer service will behave differently from one fine-tuned toward general assistance, even from the same pre-trained base.
explanation.rater-pool: A legitimate reason — module two's RLHF material established that rater preferences shape real, sometimes unintended, tendencies; different rater pools produce different tendencies.
explanation.brand-name: Not a mechanism-grounded reason at all — name recognition says nothing about what actually happened at any training stage, and it's exactly the kind of non-evidence this module is built to steer you away from relying on.

contentSections.synthesis: The three legitimate reasons all trace back to concrete training-stage choices from module two. The illegitimate one is a social signal with no mechanistic connection to actual model behavior — worth naming explicitly, because it's often the easiest signal to reach for and the least informative one.

contentSections.body: Treating model choice as irrelevant because the mechanism is shared throws away real, predictable information. It's the mirror image of a mistake this track has already named: overreaching from one true fact (shared mechanism) to a false conclusion (interchangeable outcomes) that doesn't follow from it. The accurate position holds both things at once — genuinely the same underlying process, and genuinely different, predictable results from the specific choices made while applying it. The rest of this module is about learning to evaluate those differences on evidence, rather than by reputation or by which name is more familiar.
Evaluate model differences by tracing them to real training-stage choices, not by which name you've heard of most — that's the whole discipline this module is building toward.

title: Big, small, fast, cheap: the real trade-off
description: "Bigger is always better" and "cheaper is always fine" are both wrong defaults — the real trade-off has to be evaluated against what a specific task actually requires.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate the size/cost/speed trade-off against a specific task's actual requirements
Identify the concrete costs of defaulting to the largest available model for every task

contentSections.body: A team building a high-volume feature — classifying thousands of support tickets a day — has to choose between a large, capable, slower model and a smaller, cheaper, faster one. Neither "always pick the biggest" nor "always pick the cheapest" survives contact with a real decision.

contentSections.scenario: A team defaults to the largest, most capable model available for a simple five-category ticket classification task, reasoning "bigger is always better, so why risk it." The feature works fine, but costs and response times are noticeably higher than a comparable competitor's version of the same feature.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely explanation for the unnecessary cost?

options.label: The task genuinely required the largest model's full capability, and the cost is simply unavoidable

A five-category classification task likely doesn't need the largest model's full capability, and the team paid for capability the task never used — a smaller, cheaper, faster model may well perform this specific task just as accurately
The largest model is always the cheapest option per request at scale

feedback.required: This assumes the conclusion without testing it — the whole point of this lesson is that this assumption needs to be checked against the actual task, not taken as given because the task exists.
feedback.overpaid: Right. Simple classification into a small number of categories is exactly the kind of task that often doesn't require frontier-level capability — the team is very plausibly paying a real, ongoing cost premium for capability this specific task doesn't use.
feedback.always-cheapest: Larger, more capable models are typically more expensive per token generated, not cheaper — this contradicts how model pricing generally works.

contentSections.mechanism: **Defaulting to the largest model 'to be safe' isn't actually safe — it's an untested assumption that the task needs that capability, paid for on every single request regardless of whether it's true.** The safe move is testing the assumption, not assuming it.

contentSections.body: "Bigger is always better" and "cheapest is always fine" are both untested defaults — the right choice depends on what the specific task actually requires, which has to be checked, not assumed.

contentSections.title: The costs that add up silently

contentSections.body: A product with many features, all routed through the same largest available model "to be safe," pays a cost that's easy to miss because it's spread thin across every single request rather than showing up as one obvious bill.

contentSections.scenario: A product has three features: (1) a live-typing autocomplete suggestion shown as the user types, (2) a monthly report summarizing a user's account activity in detail, (3) a high-stakes contract clause review flagging legal risks.
contentSections.question: Which feature has the strongest case for using the largest, most capable available model, even at higher cost and latency?

options.label: The live-typing autocomplete suggestion
The monthly account summary
The contract clause risk review

feedback.autocomplete: This is the strongest case for a small, fast, cheap model — users expect near-instant suggestions, and the cost of an occasional imperfect suggestion is low, while the cost of noticeable latency on every keystroke is high.
feedback.summary: A moderate case at most — this isn't real-time, so latency matters less, but it's also not especially high-stakes if occasionally imperfect, making it a reasonable candidate for a mid-tier option rather than the most expensive one.
feedback.contract: Right. Getting a legal risk assessment wrong has real, potentially serious consequences, latency is far less critical than for a live-typing feature, and this is exactly the kind of nuanced, high-stakes task where paying for the most capable available model is a defensible, evidence-based choice rather than an untested default.

contentSections.concept: **The case for the most capable, most expensive model gets stronger as stakes rise and weaker as latency sensitivity and request volume rise.** A live, high-volume, low-stakes feature and a rare, high-stakes, latency-tolerant feature call for opposite choices, from the same underlying trade-off.

contentSections.body: The cost of over-provisioning capability isn't one thing — it shows up in at least two distinct ways worth naming separately. Direct spend is the obvious one: more capable models typically cost more per token, and a high-volume feature pays that premium on every request. Latency is the less obvious one: larger models are commonly slower, and a feature where users expect a near-instant response pays a real experience cost every time it's routed through something slower than the task required. Neither cost shows up as a single alarming number — they accumulate quietly across thousands or millions of requests, which is exactly why the "just use the best one, to be safe" instinct is so easy to reach for without noticing what it's actually costing.

Reserve the largest, most capable model for where stakes are genuinely high and latency tolerance is genuinely there — use smaller, faster, cheaper models everywhere else, deliberately, not by accident.

title: Benchmarks and what they don't tell you
description: A benchmark score is real evidence, and it's routinely over-trusted — this lesson works through exactly what it does and doesn't tell you about performance on your actual task.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate what a benchmark score does and doesn't establish about real-world task performance
Identify missing context that would change how much to trust a reported benchmark score

contentSections.body: "Model A scores 91% on this benchmark, Model B scores 84%" reads like a settled comparison. It's real information — and it's answering a narrower question than the way it's usually presented implies.

contentSections.scenario: Public benchmarks typically consist of a fixed, specific set of test tasks — math problems, reading comprehension questions, coding challenges, and similar — designed and published in advance, sometimes years before newer models are evaluated against them.
contentSections.question: Roughly how much of a typical product's real, varied day-to-day usage do you think closely resembles the specific task types found in any single popular benchmark — as a rough percentage?
contentSections.explanation: There's no single correct number here — it varies enormously by product and by benchmark — but the honest estimate for most real products is low, often a small fraction of actual usage. Real usage tends to be far more varied, ambiguous, and context-specific than a fixed, pre-designed benchmark task set, which is exactly why a benchmark score is a narrower signal than it's often treated as.

contentSections.body: A benchmark is a fixed, specific set of tasks, evaluated the same way for every model that's tested on it. That specificity is what makes it useful at all — it allows a real, controlled comparison rather than vague impressions. But it's also exactly what limits what the score can tell you: it tells you how a model performs on *that particular set of tasks*, not on tasks in general, and not necessarily on your particular task, which may look nothing like what the benchmark tests. A model that's genuinely excellent at competitive-programming-style problems isn't guaranteed to be equally excellent at, say, drafting warm, on-brand customer emails — these are different skills, and a single headline benchmark score usually reflects only one of them.

contentSections.scenario: You're deciding how much weight to put on a benchmark comparison between two models for your specific product feature (drafting customer support replies).
contentSections.question: Which of these are legitimate limitations to weigh, given this lesson so far?

items.label: The benchmark's specific tasks may not resemble drafting customer support replies at all
Benchmark-similar content may have specifically influenced training in ways that inflate the score without necessarily improving general capability
Benchmark scores are always literally fabricated and never based on any real evaluation
A single score is a snapshot from one evaluation run, and doesn't capture variance across different phrasings or repeated attempts at similar tasks

explanation.task-mismatch: A real, central limitation — this is the core issue with treating any benchmark score as directly predictive of a different, specific real-world task.
explanation.contamination: A real, documented concern in the field — benchmark contamination and overfitting are genuine risks that can inflate a score's apparent meaning.
explanation.no-real-numbers: This overstates the problem — benchmark scores are generally based on real evaluations, just evaluations with real, specific limitations, not fabrications.
explanation.single-snapshot: A real, often-overlooked limitation — a single reported score doesn't capture how much performance varies across slightly different phrasings of similar tasks, which matters for a real product facing varied real user input.

contentSections.synthesis: The genuine limitations all point the same direction: a benchmark score is real evidence about a specific, narrow slice of performance, not a general verdict — treating it as the latter is the overreach worth avoiding.

contentSections.body: A benchmark score tells you about performance on that benchmark's specific tasks — real evidence, narrower scope than it's usually presented with.
A marketing page shows one impressive number with no further context. What's missing from that page is often more informative than the number itself.

contentSections.code: Marketing claim: "Our model achieves 94% on [benchmark name] — the highest score of any model in its class." (No further detail provided about the benchmark's content, evaluation methodology, or who conducted the evaluation.)
contentSections.question: What's the single most important missing piece of context here?

options.label: Whether the evaluation was independently conducted or self-reported by the company selling the model, and under what documented methodology
The exact font size used to display the number on the page
Nothing is missing — a headline score is sufficient on its own

contentSections.flawExplanation: A number with no stated methodology and no indication of independent verification is close to unfalsifiable — there's no way to judge whether the evaluation was conducted fairly, whether the benchmark's tasks resemble anything relevant, or whether the comparison to "other models in its class" used the same conditions for all of them. This isn't an accusation that the number is false — it's a statement that a bare number, presented without methodology, doesn't give you enough to actually trust it as evidence for your specific decision.

contentSections.body: None of this means benchmarks are useless — treating them as one input among several, alongside independently reported evaluations and, most importantly, your own testing against your actual task (the subject of the next lesson), is the accurate way to use them. The failure mode this lesson is specifically arguing against is treating a single headline number, especially one presented without methodology by the same party selling the model, as a settled verdict.
Weigh a benchmark score by what it actually measured and who measured it — a bare number with no methodology is weaker evidence than it's usually presented as.

title: Testing a model on your own work
description: The direct payoff of the last two lessons: neither benchmarks nor reputation substitute for actually testing candidate models against your own real task, with criteria defined before you look at the results.

learningObjectives.text: Apply a structured testing approach to compare models on a real task
Design an evaluation setup with criteria defined before seeing results

contentSections.title: The only evidence that's actually about your task

contentSections.body: Two lessons have now argued that neither raw size, nor cost, nor a headline benchmark, tells you reliably which model fits your specific task. What's actually left as reliable evidence?

contentSections.scenario: A team spends a long time debating which model to use based on published benchmark scores and general reputation, without running a single real example of their actual task through any of the candidates.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely gap in their decision-making process, given the last two lessons?

options.label: They've weighed indirect, general evidence (benchmarks, reputation) heavily, without ever gathering the one kind of evidence that's directly about their specific task — actually running it
There's no gap — benchmarks and reputation are sufficient on their own for any decision
The team should have ignored benchmarks entirely from the start

feedback.missing-direct-evidence: Right. Benchmarks and reputation are legitimate starting signals, established in the previous lesson, but they're indirect — evidence about a different task or about general perception, not about this specific task. The direct evidence (does this model actually do our task well) has never been gathered.
feedback.no-gap: The previous lesson specifically established real limitations in what benchmarks and reputation can tell you about a specific, different task — treating them as sufficient on their own repeats exactly the overreach that lesson warned against.
feedback.ignore-entirely: The previous lesson's actual position was that benchmarks are real, informative evidence, just not sufficient on their own — ignoring them entirely throws away a legitimate starting signal for narrowing candidates worth testing.

contentSections.mechanism: **Indirect evidence (benchmarks, size, reputation) is useful for narrowing which models are worth testing — it's not a substitute for direct evidence (testing the actual task).** A decision built entirely on indirect evidence skips the step that's actually informative.

contentSections.body: Benchmarks and reputation can narrow the field — only running your own real task through the candidates actually answers the question you're asking.

contentSections.title: Building a test that's actually defensible

contentSections.body: "I tried a couple of prompts and Model A seemed better" isn't nothing, but it's a much weaker claim than it's usually treated as — this pod is about the difference.

contentSections.problem: You need to choose between two candidate models for summarizing customer feedback into three bullet points. Design a testing setup that would actually produce a defensible answer.

steps.label: Gather a representative sample, not one example
steps.work: Collect at least several distinct real feedback examples spanning the range your task actually sees — different lengths, sentiments, and clarity levels.
steps.why: One example tells you about that one example — real tasks are varied, and a defensible comparison needs to reflect that variety, not one cherry-picked case.

steps.label: Write scoring criteria before running anything
steps.work: Define, in writing, what a good summary looks like: captures main sentiment, includes any specific actionable complaint, genuinely stays to three bullets, invents no detail absent from the original.
steps.why: Criteria written after seeing outputs risk being unconsciously shaped to favor whichever output already looks better — writing them first keeps the comparison honest.

steps.label: Hold settings constant across candidates
steps.work: Use the same temperature and any system instruction for every model being tested.
steps.why: If settings differ between candidates, you can't tell whether a difference in output came from the model itself or from an unrelated settings difference — module four's material applies directly here.

steps.label: Score against the criteria, blind if possible
steps.work: Evaluate each output against the written criteria, ideally without knowing in advance which model produced which output.
steps.why: Removing the knowledge of which model produced which output reduces the risk of unconsciously favoring a model you expected to perform better.

faded.problem: Apply the same structure to a different case: choosing between three candidate models for drafting polite decline emails to job applicants.

blanks.prompt: What should you gather first — one example, or several representative ones?
blanks.why: Same logic — a single test case doesn't reflect the range of real applicant situations this task will actually face.

blanks.prompt: When should the scoring criteria (e.g. 'polite but clear, no false hope, correct name used') be written — before or after seeing the outputs?
blanks.why: Writing criteria first prevents them from being unconsciously shaped by which output already looks better.

blanks.prompt: Should the three candidate models be tested with different settings, or the same settings?
blanks.why: Different settings would make it impossible to isolate whether a difference in output came from the model itself or the settings.

blanks.prompt: Should you know which model produced which output while scoring, or should scoring be blind?
blanks.why: Blind scoring reduces the risk of favoring a model based on reputation rather than the actual output quality.

contentSections.procedure: **Representative sample → criteria written first → settings held constant → blind scoring where possible.** This is the same rigor as the module four lab, applied to comparing models instead of comparing settings on one model.

contentSections.body: A defensible model comparison looks like an actual experiment — representative examples, criteria set in advance, controlled settings, and scoring that doesn't already know the answer it wants.

title: Local models: what's actually possible on your machine
description: Running a model locally trades real capability (per the size trade-off from earlier in this module) for real, concrete benefits — privacy, no per-request cost, no external dependency — and deciding between them takes the same evidence-based evaluation this module has built throughout.

learningObjectives.text: Explain the real trade-off between locally-run and hosted models
Evaluate whether a local model is the right choice for a specific, concrete use case

contentSections.title: What running locally actually trades away and gains

contentSections.body: A model that runs entirely on your own computer, no internet connection required once downloaded, no data ever leaving the machine, no per-request bill. That sounds like a strict upgrade — and the size trade-off from earlier in this module says it can't be.

contentSections.question: Given that data-center hardware hosting the largest frontier models is far more powerful than a typical personal computer, what does that predict about how capable a model you can practically run entirely locally will be, compared to the largest hosted options?
contentSections.answer: Practically limited — a model that has to run on much more modest local hardware is typically smaller and, per the size/capability trade-off from earlier in this module, generally less capable on genuinely difficult tasks than the largest hosted frontier models running on data-center-scale infrastructure.
contentSections.hint: This is the exact same size/capability relationship from lesson two, just applied to a hardware constraint instead of a deliberate product choice.

contentSections.body: Local models are a genuinely real, useful option, not a novelty — and they come with a real trade-off, not a free upgrade. The benefits are concrete: data never leaves the machine, which matters enormously for anything with genuine confidentiality requirements; there's no per-request cost once the model is downloaded and running; and there's no dependence on an external service staying available, priced the same, or unchanged in behavior over time. The cost is equally concrete: practical hardware limits on a typical personal machine mean a locally-runnable model is generally smaller than the largest hosted options, and per this module's earlier lessons, smaller generally means a real capability gap on genuinely difficult tasks — not a rule without exception, but a real pattern worth taking seriously rather than assuming away.

Local models trade real capability, per the size/capability relationship from this module, for real, concrete benefits — privacy, no per-request cost, no external dependency. Neither side of that trade is free.

A small business handling sensitive customer documents has to actually decide, not just acknowledge that there's a trade-off — this pod is about applying the whole module's evaluation discipline to one concrete case.

contentSections.scenario:
Three use cases considering a locally-run model over a hosted one:

1. A hobbyist experimenting with creative writing prompts, no sensitive data involved
2. A clinic processing patient records with strict confidentiality requirements, where task accuracy on record summarization has been tested and found close to comparable between local and hosted options
3. A startup needing state-of-the-art performance on a genuinely difficult, novel research task, with no particular privacy sensitivity
contentSections.question: Which of these has the strongest case for choosing the local option specifically because of its privacy benefit outweighing a capability gap?

options.label: Case 1 — the hobbyist
Case 2 — the clinic
Case 3 — the startup

feedback.1: The hobbyist has no real privacy stakes driving the decision — the choice here would come down mostly to convenience and capability, not the privacy benefit specifically.
feedback.2: Right. Genuine confidentiality requirements (patient records) plus tested, comparable accuracy on the specific task is exactly the profile where the local option's privacy benefit is doing real work and the capability trade-off has been specifically shown not to be a problem for this task.
feedback.3: This case explicitly needs state-of-the-art performance on a genuinely difficult task with no privacy sensitivity driving the decision — the capability trade-off matters most here and there's no privacy benefit to offset it, making the hosted option the stronger case.

contentSections.concept: **The case for a local model strengthens with genuine privacy stakes and weakens with genuine need for maximum capability — deciding well means checking both, specifically, for the actual use case, not defaulting to either option.**

contentSections.body: This closes out the module on the same note it opened with: every comparison in this whole module — model to model, size to size, benchmark to real testing, hosted to local — comes down to checking specific, concrete factors against a specific, real task rather than reaching for a general rule that decides it for you. That discipline, more than any single fact about any single model, is what this module has actually been teaching.

Choosing between local and hosted, like every other comparison this module covered, comes down to weighing real, specific factors against the actual task — not defaulting to either option out of habit.
