title: Lab — Run Your Own Model Comparison on a Real Task
description: The module's argument, put into practice: pick a real task, compare at least two real models on it with proper method, and produce a recommendation you could actually defend.

learningObjectives.text: Design and execute a defensible comparison between at least two models on a real task
Produce a stated, evidence-based recommendation

contentSections.body: This module has spent five lessons arguing that model choice should be evidence-based, not reputation-based. This lab is where you actually build that evidence, on a real task of your own choosing.

contentSections.title: Your own model comparison
contentSections.brief: Choose a real task you'd genuinely want help with. Compare at least two different models (different providers, different sizes within a family, or a hosted model versus a local one if you have access) against that real task, using the structured method from this module, and produce a stated recommendation with reasoning.
contentSections.deliverable: A comparison of at least two models tested on the same representative set of real examples from your chosen task, scored against criteria you wrote in advance, with a final stated recommendation and the reasoning behind it.

stages.title: Choose the task and write criteria first
stages.instructions: Pick a real, specific task — something you'd actually use a model for. Before running anything, write down what a good output looks like for this task: 3-5 concrete, checkable criteria. Also decide which two (or more) models you're comparing and why they're worth comparing for this task.
stages.checkpoint: You have a specific task, written criteria, and a stated reason for choosing the specific models being compared — all written before any output has been generated.

stages.title: Gather representative examples and run the comparison
stages.instructions: Gather at least three to five representative real examples of your task — enough to see a pattern, not just one lucky or unlucky case. Run the identical examples through each candidate model, using the same settings across all of them. Save every output in full.
stages.checkpoint: You have the same set of representative examples run through every candidate model, with all outputs saved and clearly labeled by which model produced them.

stages.title: Score, compare, and recommend
stages.instructions: Score every output against the criteria you wrote in stage one. Build a simple comparison (a table works well) showing how each model performed against each criterion. Write a final recommendation: which model you'd actually use for this task, and why, referencing specific evidence from your comparison rather than a general impression. If cost, speed, or privacy were relevant factors for this task, factor them into the recommendation explicitly.
stages.checkpoint: You have a completed comparison table, a specific recommendation, and reasoning that references actual evidence from the comparison rather than a general impression.

rubric.criterion: The task is real and specific
rubric.meets: The chosen task is something genuinely useful to the learner, described specifically, not a generic placeholder.

rubric.criterion: Criteria were written before seeing any output
rubric.meets: The written criteria are visibly separate from, and precede, the actual model outputs — not adjusted afterward to fit what happened.

rubric.criterion: At least two models were tested on identical, representative examples
rubric.meets: The same set of at least three representative examples was run through each candidate model, with all outputs included in full.

rubric.criterion: Settings were held constant across candidates
rubric.meets: The comparison used the same settings (temperature, any system instruction) across all models tested, so differences in output can be attributed to the model rather than settings.

rubric.criterion: The recommendation is evidence-based
rubric.meets: The final recommendation explicitly references specific results from the comparison, not just a general preference or reputation.

rubric.criterion: Relevant non-accuracy factors are addressed if applicable
rubric.meets: If cost, speed, or privacy genuinely mattered for this task, the recommendation explicitly weighs them, not just raw output quality.

contentSections.body: Running one real, evidence-based comparison — with criteria set before you looked at results — is worth more than any amount of reading about which model is supposedly best in general.

title: Checkpoint — Different Models, Different Jobs
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four reaching back to settings, two reaching further back to training. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's model-evaluation mechanisms alongside earlier modules' material

questions.from: This module — Different Models, Different Jobs
questions.prompt: Why can two models sharing the exact same underlying mechanism still behave meaningfully differently?

options.label: The specific training-stage choices — data composition, fine-tuning targets, RLHF rater pools — differ between them, producing different learned statistics
One of them must not really be using next-token prediction
They don't actually behave differently in practice

questions.explanation: Same mechanism, different inputs at every training stage, different results.

questions.from: This module — Different Models, Different Jobs
questions.prompt: What's the accurate way to weigh a headline benchmark score when choosing a model for a specific task?

options.label: It should be the sole deciding factor
It's real evidence about performance on that benchmark's specific task set, which may not resemble your actual task — informative but not a substitute for testing your own task
Benchmark scores should be ignored entirely

questions.explanation: A benchmark measures a fixed, specific task set — genuinely informative, narrower in scope than it's often presented as.

questions.from: This module — Different Models, Different Jobs
questions.prompt: What's the most reliable way to know which model suits your specific real task?

options.label: Pick the model with the highest overall benchmark average
Run your own representative examples of the actual task through candidate models, scored against criteria written in advance
Pick whichever model is most recently released

questions.explanation: Direct evidence about your actual task beats indirect evidence like benchmarks or recency.

questions.from: This module — Different Models, Different Jobs
questions.prompt: What's the real trade-off of running a model locally instead of through a hosted API?

options.label: There's no trade-off, local is strictly better
Genuine benefits (privacy, no per-request cost, no external dependency) alongside a genuine capability trade-off, since locally-runnable models are typically smaller than the largest hosted options
Local models have no real advantages at all

questions.explanation: A real trade-off in both directions, following directly from the size/capability relationship covered earlier in the module.

questions.from: Previous module — The Settings That Change the Output
questions.prompt: What does temperature actually control?

options.label: How the probability distribution over the next token gets sampled from
How many tokens the model is allowed to generate in total
Whether the model follows a system instruction

questions.explanation: Temperature is applied to the probability distribution before a token is sampled — a sampling-behavior setting.

questions.from: Previous module — The Settings That Change the Output
questions.prompt: Mechanistically, what makes a system instruction different from an ordinary user message?

options.label: It's processed by a completely separate, hardcoded enforcement system
Both are tokens in the same context window; training specifically teaches the model to weight system-role content as higher-priority framing
System instructions are invisible to the model itself

questions.explanation: Same mechanism, training-shaped weighting — not a separate enforcement layer.

questions.from: Previous module — The Settings That Change the Output
questions.prompt: Why does a response sometimes cut off mid-sentence with an unclosed bracket?

options.label: The model decided that was a good stopping point
An external maximum output length limit was hit before the model reached its own natural stopping point
The topic was too difficult

questions.explanation: A clean ending and a mid-structure cutoff are two different mechanisms.

questions.from: Previous module — The Settings That Change the Output
questions.prompt: What does reasoning mode actually do, mechanistically?

options.label: Switches to a fundamentally different computational process separate from token prediction
Generates additional intermediate tokens (a scratchpad of reasoning steps) before the final answer, using the same next-token prediction mechanism throughout
Replaces prediction with a symbolic logic solver

questions.explanation: Same mechanism, more prediction steps — not a new kind of computation.

questions.from: Three modules back — Where the Behaviour Comes From
questions.prompt: Why can RLHF produce sycophancy without anyone training for it directly?

options.label: Raters, comparing responses without independently fact-checking every claim, tend to find agreement more pleasant than correction on average, and that preference shapes the reward signal
Sycophancy is explicitly written into the reward model's objective
It only happens with poorly-trained reward models

questions.explanation: A predictable byproduct of optimizing for aggregate preference rather than a direct measure of truth.

questions.from: Three modules back — Where the Behaviour Comes From
questions.prompt: Why can't a single later training pass fully remove bias from a model?

options.label: Bias can enter independently at multiple stages — corpus composition, fine-tuning example selection, and the rater pool
Bias is impossible to address at any stage
A single pass actually can remove it completely

questions.explanation: Each training stage is an independent opportunity for skew to enter.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.
